The Qur'an usually uses it in this very sense, as in *"we used to indulge (in vain discourse) with those indulging"* (74:45) and *"playing with what they are indulged in"* (6:91). The image is of people wading and splashing about in what is sacred, for sport. The scholars Maulana Ashraf Ali Thanavi and Shaykh al-Hind, Maulana Mahmud al-Hasan, rendered the phrase in the sense of fault-finding and disputing: people meddling in the Ayat of Allah just for fun and ridicule, or trying to find faults in them.

Two details in the command matter. First, its scope: Ibn Kathir states plainly that "this command includes every member of this Ummah" — no one is to sit with those who deny and distort Allah's Ayat and explain them incorrectly. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a beautiful observation: the address is directed to the Prophet ﷺ only so that the Muslims at large would hear it, for he himself never participated in any such gatherings even in his childhood days, and so needed no prohibition. Second, its limit: the withdrawal lasts *"till they turn to another topic"* — until they talk about a subject other than the denial they were engaged in. The ban is not on the people absolutely but on the session of mockery — though, as we will see, the scholars drew the circle wider for habitual scoffers.

Both Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān link this ayah to its counterpart: *"when you hear the Verses of Allah being denied and mocked at, then sit not with them, until they engage in a talk other than that; (but if you stayed with them) certainly in that case you would be like them"* (4:140). Ibn Kathir's gloss is sobering: if you still sit with them, agreeing to what they say, you will be just like them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the underlying reason as a matter of principle: a sin is a sin, whether you do it yourself or watch others doing it.

## What "turning away" requires — the scholars' rulings

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the practical law here with unusual care.

**How to turn away.** In principle, "turning away" could take many forms — leaving the gathering, or getting busy with something else while there and paying the mockers no attention. But the end of the ayah makes clear that the first form is what is desirable: one should not keep sitting in their gathering; one should rise and leave. Imam al-Razi in Tafsir Kabir adds a merciful qualification: if leaving the gathering would pose a danger to one's life, property, or honour, it is permissible for common people to "turn away" in some other manner — for instance, busying themselves with something else and paying no attention. But the case is different with particular people who are followed in religious matters; for them, the only appropriate way is to rise and leave the gathering.

**When staying is permitted.** Imam al-Jassas, in Ahkam al-Qur'an, says this verse tells that Muslims should abstain from every gathering where things are being said against Allah, His Rasul ﷺ, and the Shari'ah of Islam, when it is not within one's power to stop it or at least to say what is true and right. However, participating in such a gathering with the intention to reform and to carry the message of truth to them does not matter.

**How far the prohibition reaches.** From the closing words — *"then after the remembrance, sit not you in the company of those people who are the wrongdoers"* — al-Jassas deduces a stricter ruling: participating in the gathering of such unjust, irreligious, and big-mouthed people is an absolute sin, whether or not they are engaged in the impermissible talk at that moment, because people of such nature could be expected to start their ridiculous rantings all of a sudden. The verse prohibits sitting with them in an absolute sense, without the condition that they be busy with their offence at the time. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the same subject is taken up more explicitly in another verse: *"And do not incline towards the wrong doers, lest the Fire should catch you"* (11:113).

## "And if Shaytan makes you forget" — can a prophet forget?

The ayah anticipates human weakness: one may wander into such a gathering unmindfully. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān specifies the two ways this happens — either not remembering the prohibition of participating in such gatherings, or not recalling that these particular people talk against the Ayat of Allah and His Rasul ﷺ in their sittings. In either situation, once it is remembered, one must leave that gathering immediately; to keep sitting there after having remembered is a sin.

But if the address includes the Prophet ﷺ, a theological question arises, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān faces it directly: if forgetfulness can affect a prophet and messenger of Allah, how can his teachings be trusted? The answer given: it is possible that prophets too forget something under particular circumstances, where the divine wisdom decides to make it happen for a particular purpose — but they are immediately alerted by Allah through *waḥy* (revelation), so the lapse is never allowed to last. Their teachings therefore remain free of any doubt of forgetfulness.

For the rest of us, the phrase carries a consolation. Both commentaries cite here the Prophet's ﷺ saying that removed from this Ummah is unintentional error, forgetfulness, and what one is coerced to do. Wandering in unawares is forgiven; lingering after you remember is not.

## The Companions' question — and the mercy of ayah 69

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān preserves the moment that produced ayah 69. When the prohibition came down, the noble Companions submitted: Ya Rasul Allah, if this absolute prohibition of going into their gatherings remained in force, we shall be deprived of offering Salah and Tawaf in al-Masjid al-Haram, because these people keep sitting there all the time doing nothing but fault-finding and ill-speaking. (The commentary notes in passing that this was the situation before the Hijrah and the Conquest of Makkah.) Thereupon the next verse was revealed: *"There is no responsibility for them upon those who have Taqwa, but (their duty) is to remind them, that they may (attain) Taqwa."*

*Taqwa* is the operative word — rendered in the translation given here as being "mindful of Allah," and by Maʿārif ul Qurʼān as observing restraint. The ayah means, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, that when people who observe restraint go to al-Masjid al-Haram for their own rightful purpose, they are not responsible for the evil deeds of those wicked people present there. Ibn Kathir reads the same clause as reassurance for those who obey ayah 68: by avoiding the wrongdoers' sittings they are innocent of them and have saved themselves from their sin.

Yet the ayah does not license cold indifference. Its final clause keeps a duty alive: it remains the believers' duty to tell them what is right and true, which may perhaps help them take the right path. Ibn Kathir adds that even the act of shunning them is itself part of the reminder: the believers were commanded to ignore and avoid them precisely "so that they become aware of the error they are indulging in," that they may avoid this behavior and never repeat it. The withdrawal is not contempt; it is itself a form of preaching.

## Religion as a game, and the Day no ransom is taken (70)

Ayah 70 widens the lens from the gathering to the people themselves: *"And leave alone those who take their religion as play and amusement, and are deceived by the life of this world."*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up the wording. The word *dhar* is derived from *wadhara*, which means being displeased with something and leaving it — not a neutral departure. And the phrase about taking religion as play bears two readings, both true: either they turned the true religion sent to them — Islam — into a plaything and a laughing stock; or they left their real faith and took fun and play as their very own religion and purpose of life. The outcome of both meanings, the commentary notes, is nearly the same.

Then the diagnosis: the transitory life of the present world has deceived them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls this "a true diagnosis of their real problem" — they are so disobedient and wicked only because they are bewitched by the glamour of their mortal life, totally forgetting the state of life ahead of them; had they believed in the Akhirah and the Last Day, they would never have acted so recklessly.

Note that the command to leave them is paired with its opposite: *"But remind (them) with it"* — with the Qur'an. Ibn Kathir explains: remind the people with this Qur'an and warn them against Allah's revenge and painful torment on the Day of Resurrection. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān stresses that the Prophet ﷺ and the Muslims are given two orders at once: avoid these people, and yet act positively — continue preaching through the Qur'an and keep putting the fear of Allah's punishment in their hearts. Avoidance is a boundary, not an abdication.

The reason for the reminder is *"lest a soul Tubsal for that which one has earned."* Ibn Kathir gathers the early authorities on this rare word: Ad-Dahhak reported from Ibn 'Abbas — along with Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, Al-Hasan and As-Suddi — that it means to be submissive; Al-Walibi reported that Ibn 'Abbas said "be exposed"; Qatadah said "be prevented"; Murrah and Ibn Zayd said "be recompensed"; Al-Kalbi said "be reckoned." Ibn Kathir concludes that all these expressions are similar: they mean exposure to destruction, being kept away from all that is good, and being restrained from attaining what is desired. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it "to be detained or be entrapped" — the soul held by its own earnings, as Allah says elsewhere: *"Every person is restrained by what he has earned"* (74:38).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then draws a piercing sketch of why the ayah lists what it lists. In this world a guilty man is accustomed to rely on three escape routes: the power and influence of his party or group; failing that, recommendations from influential people; failing that, money. The ayah closes all three. No friend or relative can save Allah's criminal from punishment; no intercession by anyone can succeed without the permission of Allah; and no wealth of any kind will be accepted — even if the criminal possessed the wealth of the whole world and offered it all, this *fidyah* (ransom) would not be accepted from him. As the ayah says, *"even if he offers every ransom, it will not be accepted from him"* — and Ibn Kathir cites the parallel: were a disbeliever to offer the whole earth full of gold, it would not be accepted (3:91). The ayah ends with the sentence itself: for them will be a drink of boiling water — about which another verse says that it will shatter their entrails apart (47:15) — and a painful torment, because they used to disbelieve.

## Living it: company is destiny

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the essential objective of ayat 68–70 in one line: to save Muslims from evil environment and bad company, "which can be as deadly as poison." It observes that many clear and conclusive statements of the Qur'an and Hadith, as well as repeated observation and experience, prove that the root of all evils and crimes people fall into is the evil society and environment in which they grow up. Once snared, a person slides into evils against his own grain and conscience; then habit sets in and the very sense of evil dies away — until he starts taking evil as good and good as evil. The Prophet ﷺ is reported to have said that when a person commits a sin for the first time, a dot appears on his heart — like a black dot on a white dress, which everyone dislikes, so that he too feels the distaste in his heart. But as he goes on to the second and the third sin without repenting from the past one, black dots keep appearing, one after another, until the radiant tablet of the heart turns jet black — and he is deprived of the very ability to distinguish between good and bad. The Qur'an identifies this with the word *rān* (rust, stain) in 83:14, which the commentary explains to mean that there is rust on their hearts because of their evil deeds, which has taken away their ability to receive good.

The commentary also warns, from this very verse, that the company of people who are heedless of the Akhirah and content with their mortal life is fatal for everyone — whoever sits in their company shall be subject to the same punishment in which they are caught. Hence its closing counsel: may Allah keep us all protected from wrong environment and bad company, and everyone responsible for raising children must do their best to keep them safe from such society and environment.

The balance of the whole passage is its beauty. The Prophet ﷺ is taught to say, *"I am not responsible for your affairs"* (ayah 66), and every denied warning has its set time to transpire (ayah 67). So the believer neither argues in the mud nor abandons the mockers to it: rise from the gathering (ayah 68), remain untainted while still reminding (ayah 69), and keep the Qur'an sounding in their hearing, lest any soul be seized by what its own hands have earned (ayah 70).

passages.title: Only submission to the Lord of all worlds
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat are the believer's scripted answer to an invitation to turn back. The previous passage (68–70) commanded the Prophet ﷺ and the Muslims to avoid people who had taken their faith as game and play; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that verses 71–73 likewise deal with the refutation of *shirk* (setting up partners with Allah) and the affirmation of *tawhid* (His absolute Oneness) and of the Hereafter. What binds the three together is a single movement: from the false call that tries to pull a believer off the road (71), to the one true call and the creed it demands (71–72), to the Day on which every call will be settled by the Lord whose word is truth (73).

## The invitation these verses answer

Ibn Kathir records the occasion from as-Suddi, in a statement Ibn Jarir recorded: some idolaters said to some Muslims, "Follow us and abandon the religion of Muhammad." Allah then sent down this revelation. So the "Say" that opens ayah 71 is not an abstract theology lesson — it is Allah putting the reply into the believers' mouths.

And what a reply it is. "Shall we invoke, besides Allah, what can neither benefit us nor harm us?" The question exposes the emptiness of the offer before refusing it. These so-called gods fail the most elementary test of a deity: they can do nothing for you and nothing against you. And "shall we turn on our heels" — explained in Ibn Kathir's tafsir as reverting to disbelief — "after Allah has guided us?" To accept the idolaters' invitation would not be broad-mindedness; it would be walking backwards out of light one has already been given.

## The parable of the lost traveller

Ayah 71 then paints the picture that carries the whole passage. As-Suddi unfolds it: a man sets out with companions on a road. He loses his way, and the devils lead him wandering in confusion across the land. All the while his companions on the road are calling him: "Come back to us, for we are on the path." But he refuses. This, said as-Suddi, is the example of the one who follows the devil after recognising Muhammad ﷺ — and Muhammad ﷺ is the person calling the people to the path, and the path is Islam.

Ibn Kathir then dwells on the wording of the ayah itself — "like one whom the devils have made to go astray, wandering through the land" — which, he says, refers to ghouls, calling the lost man *by his own name, his father's name, and his grandfather's name*. He follows the devils' call thinking it is a path of guidance, and by morning he finds himself destroyed — perhaps they eat him; the Jinns then leave him to wander in a wasteland, where he dies of thirst. Such, the exposition says, is the example of those who follow the false gods worshipped instead of Allah, Most Honored. Ibn Jarir also recorded this.

That detail deserves a pause. In the parable, misguidance does not announce itself as misguidance; it calls the traveller by his own name, his father's and his grandfather's names — familiar, personal, plausible. He follows the voice thinking it is the way to guidance, and it leads him to destruction. The parable's warning is plain: a familiar voice in the dark is not the same thing as the road home.

## Only one guidance

Against the many voices in the wilderness, ayah 71 sets down a single sentence: "Say: Verily, Allah's guidance is the only guidance." Not one option among several — *the* guidance. Ibn Kathir pairs this with Allah's words elsewhere: "And whomsoever Allah guides, for him there will be none to misguide him" (39:37), and "If you covet for their guidance, then verily Allah guides not those whom He makes to go astray. And they will have no helpers" (16:37). Guidance is Allah's to give; no devil can undo it for the one He guides, and no eager preacher can supply it to the one He has left to stray.

## The creed in three commands

Having refused the false call, the passage states what the believers were called *to*. "We have been commanded to submit to the Lord of all worlds" — and Ibn Kathir defines this submission precisely: to worship Allah in sincerity, to Him alone, without partners. This is the passage's title-thought: *islam* itself, surrender, offered not to a tribe or a tradition but to the Lord of everything that exists.

Ayah 72 then gives that surrender its daily shape: "and to establish the prayer (*salah*), and have *taqwa* of Him." *Taqwa* is the vigilant, protective fear-and-mindfulness of Allah; Ibn Kathir notes that the command is to fear Him "in all circumstances" — not only in the mosque, not only when watched. And the verse seals the creed with its final motive: "and it is He to Whom you shall be gathered" — on the Day of Resurrection, as Ibn Kathir specifies. Notice the arc across these two ayat: inward surrender, then outward practice, then constant consciousness of Allah, then the final accounting. That is the whole religion in one breath — and it is the road the companions were calling the lost man back to.

## The Day when He says "Be"

Ayah 73 grounds all of this in who Allah actually is. "It is He Who created the heavens and the earth in truth" — Ibn Kathir explains "in truth" as meaning *in justice*: He is their Originator and Owner, who governs their affairs and the affairs of their inhabitants. The heavens and the earth were made with truth, by a Lord who owns them and rules them justly.

"And on the Day He will say: 'Be!' and it shall become." Ibn Kathir reads this of the Day of Resurrection: when Allah says to it "Be," it will come faster than the blink of an eye. One command, and the Hour is here — nothing needs to be assembled or negotiated. "His Word is the truth": the same verse that names Him Creator of the heavens and the earth names His promise of that Day as truth.

## The Trumpet

"His will be the dominion on the Day when the *Sur* is blown." Ibn Kathir offers two ways of connecting this clause: either "the Day the Sur is blown" refers to His statement "on the Day He will say: 'Be!' and it shall become," or the sense is "His will be the dominion on the Day when the Sur will be blown." He supports the latter with Allah's words: "Whose is the kingdom this Day? It is Allah's, the One, the Irresistible!" (40:16), and "The sovereignty on that Day will be the true sovereignty, belonging to the Most Beneficent, and it will be a hard Day for the disbelievers" (25:26). On that Day the question of ayah 71 answers itself forever: the beings who could "neither benefit nor harm" will own nothing, and the Lord of all worlds will own everything, visibly.

What is the *Sur*? Ibn Kathir explains it is the Trumpet into which the angel Israfil, peace be upon him, will blow. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Israfil has held the Sur in his mouth and lowered his forehead, awaiting the command to blow in it" — Muslim recorded this hadith in his Sahih. And Imam Ahmad recorded that 'Abdullah bin 'Amr said: a bedouin man asked, "O Allah's Messenger! What is the Sur?" He replied: "A Trumpet which will be blown." The image is sobering: the instrument of the end of the world is already at an angel's lips, his forehead bowed, waiting only for the command. The Hour is not a distant abstraction; it is one order away.

The ayah closes by naming the One who will preside over that Day: "All-Knower of the unseen and the seen; He is the All-Wise, Well-Aware." We affirm these names as they come, as the early Muslims did — without likening Him to His creation and without explaining them away — for Allah is as He has described Himself, as befits His majesty.

## Living it

Read as a unit, the passage hands the believer two things. First, an answer — when the pull comes to drift back to what everyone around you follows, the reply is already written: *why would I call on what can neither help nor harm me, after Allah has guided me?* Second, a diagnosis — in the parable, the voice that leads to ruin calls the traveller by his own name, warm and familiar, while the true companions are the ones calling him back to the road; and the caller at the head of that road is the Prophet ﷺ. And behind both stands the reason it matters: to Him you will be gathered, on a Day already waiting on a single word.

passages.title: Abraham's search past star, moon, and sun
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat tell how Ibrahim (peace be upon him) confronted the two-layered shirk of his people — the idols they carved on earth and the lights they revered in the sky — and, through one of the most memorable arguments in the Qur'an, walked them past star, moon, and sun to the One who originated the heavens and the earth. The passage moves as a single sweep: it opens at home with a challenge to his father (ayah 74), widens into a staged public demonstration across three risings and three settings (ayat 76–78), and closes with a declaration of pure monotheism that, in the words of Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, draws "a line of demarcation" forever (ayah 79).

## Why this story is told here

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the preceding verses carried the Holy Prophet's ﷺ call to the disbelievers of Arabia to abandon idols and worship Allah alone. This passage now supports that call in a way the Arabs could not easily dismiss: Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was their own patriarch, and all Arabia stood united in paying homage to him. So this is no detour into ancient history. The Qur'an is telling Makkah: the very forefather you revere spent his life demolishing exactly what you now defend.

## Ayah 74 — the call begins at home

Ibrahim's first word of truth was spoken not in a public square but in his own house, to a respected elder of his family: "Do you take idols as gods? I see you and your people in manifest error." Ibn Kathir explains "manifest error" as wandering in confusion, not knowing where to go — an error plain to anyone of sound reason. He connects this scene to Sūrah Maryam (19:41–48), where the same conversation is given in full tenderness — "O my father, why do you worship that which hears not, sees not…" — and ends with the father threatening to stone him, and Ibrahim answering only, "Peace be on you! I will ask forgiveness of my Lord for you."

**Who was Āzar?** The commentaries record a genuine difference. It is commonly held that Āzar was the name of Ibrahim's father, while most historians give the father's name as Tārakh and treat Āzar as his title. Imam al-Rāzī and a group of early scholars held that Tārakh was the father and Āzar was in fact the *uncle*, who became a minister of Nimrūd and fell into polytheism; since Arab usage commonly calls an uncle "father", he is named as father here. Zarqānī, in Sharḥ al-Mawāhib, reported several proofs for this view. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presents these positions without forcing a single verdict — and either way, the lesson stands.

**Reform begins at home.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws from this that starting daʿwah — the work of inviting people to the truth — from one's own home and family is the way (Sunnah) of the prophets. The Holy Prophet ﷺ was commanded likewise, "And warn your near relatives" (26:214), and in obedience to it first gathered his own family at the hill of Ṣafā. And from Tafsir al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ: inviting a respected elder of the family to the right path is not contrary to reverence for him — it is the truest form of wishing him well.

## Ayah 75 — shown the kingdom before the debate

Before the demonstration with star, moon, and sun is narrated, Allah says: "Thus did We show Ibrahim the malakūt of the heavens and the earth, that he be one of those who have faith with certainty." *Malakūt* is the kingdom or dominion of creation. Ibn Kathir explains: when Ibrahim contemplated the heavens and the earth, Allah showed him in them the proofs of His Oneness — that there is no god or Lord except Allah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it beautifully: Allah made him see created things in a way that *unravelled their reality*, so that his conviction would be firm.

This verse is the key to reading everything that follows. The man who looks at the star and says "this is my lord" is not a seeker groping in the dark; he is a man to whom Allah has already shown what the heavens really are, now leading others through the same discovery.

## Ayat 76–78 — three lights, three settings

**What his people actually believed.** Ibn Kathir describes their religion in two layers. They worshipped earthly idols which they had shaped in the image of heavenly angels, hoping the angels would intercede for them with the Creator — for they thought themselves too insignificant to worship Allah directly. And they worshipped the seven planets — the Moon, Mercury, Venus, the Sun, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn — of which the most honoured were the Sun, the Moon, and Venus. Ibn Kathir identifies the *kawkab* (star) of ayah 76 as Venus, and traces Ibrahim's argument against it: Venus is bound to an appointed course it cannot defy, swerving neither right nor left, having no say in its own affairs — it rises in the east, sets in the west, and repeats the same circuit the next night. Such a thing cannot be a god.

**"This is my lord" — confusion or strategy?** Both commentaries in our sources read these words as debate, not doubt. Ibn Kathir titles the whole section "Prophet Ibrahim Debates with his People." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unfolds the tone: Ibrahim said it in the sense of *"Is this not, as you think and believe, my Lord and your Lord? In a little while you will find out how real that is."* He meets his people on their own ground, lets their god rise in full glory — and then lets the sky itself refute them. Ibn Kathir records the comment of Qatādah: "Ibrahim knew that his Lord is Eternal and never ceases."

**The star (ayah 76).** "When the night overcame him" — Ibn Kathir: covered him in darkness — "he saw a kawkab." When it *afala* — set, vanished — he said, "I do not like those that set" (*lā uḥibbu al-āfilīn*). The word *āfilīn* comes from *ufūl*, "to set." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up why this single word wins the argument: whatever is taken as an object of worship must, by definition, be supremely worthy of love and reverence — and what vanishes does not deserve to be held dear. The commentary quotes a couplet of Maulana Rūmī that makes this very line the password of faith — in its rendering: enter the Domain of Belief, like Khalīl, by proclaiming the password: "I do not like the vanishing!"

**The moon (ayah 77).** Another night, the glowing moon rises (*bāzighan*, "rising up") and the same method repeats — until it too sets, and Ibrahim says: "Unless my Lord guides me, I shall surely be among the misguided people." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān catches two things here. First, a confession wrapped in a warning: had my Rabb not been guiding me all along, I would be as astray as you, and might have taken this very moon as my god. Second, a quiet hint to his listeners: the Lord of Ibrahim is clearly some other Being altogether — One from whom guidance *keeps coming* even while the moon rises and sets.

**The sun (ayah 78).** Finally the greatest light of all: "This is my lord — this is greater (*hādhā akbar*)!" — bigger than star and moon, and more radiant, as Ibn Kathir notes. If anything in the sky deserved worship, it was this. And when it too set, the argument was complete: if the best candidate fails, every lesser one fails with it. So Ibrahim declares his *barāʼah* — his complete disassociation: "O my people, I am indeed free of all that you associate with Allah." Ibn Kathir renders the force of it: I am free of these objects and of taking them as protectors — and if they really are gods as you claim, then let all of you bring your plot against me and give me no respite.

**Why "setting" and not some other proof?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses over a subtle choice. Ibrahim could have argued from the stars' rising, or from their fixed orbits — both equally prove they are governed by another power. But he built his whole case on their *setting*, because setting spells decline in the eyes of ordinary people; everyone feels the smallness of a light that slips beneath the horizon. This, says the commentary, is the characteristic method of the prophets: they do not chase philosophical truisms but address people at the level of common comprehension, choosing the proof that actually lands in the heart.

## Ayah 79 — the face turned

The passage ends with words of surrender: "I have turned my face towards Him Who originated the heavens and the earth, ḥanīfan, and I am not of the idolaters." Ibn Kathir unpacks each phrase. "I have turned my face" — I have purified my religion and made my worship sincere. *Faṭara* — He originated and shaped the heavens and the earth without any precedent to copy. *Ḥanīf* — one who turns away from shirk and embraces tawhid, the pure worship of Allah alone. The One worshipped is He in Whose Hand is the dominion of all things — the Creator, Lord, King, and true Ilāh of all things in existence — the One who, as Ibn Kathir cites from 7:54, created "the sun, the moon, the stars, subjecting them to His command."

## "Your people" and "O my people"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notices a delicate shift in address. In ayah 74, speaking to his father, Ibrahim says "I see you and *your* people in manifest error" — declining to count himself among them. But in ayah 78, at the moment of principled disassociation, he says "O *my* people" — owning them by race and homeland even while cutting every religious tie. The hint: you remain my kin, but your disbelief has forced a parting of ways. From this the commentary derives that a believer's deepest identity is faith itself, not lineage or land. It recalls that during the journey of his Last Hajj the Holy Prophet ﷺ met a caravan and asked what people they were; they answered, "We are a nation of Muslims" (al-Bukhari) — naming no tribe, only their real nationality, the one that outlasts every other.

## What became of the father

Ibn Kathir completes the human story. Ibrahim went on asking forgiveness for his father all his father's life, because of a promise he had made him; but when the father died an idolater and this became clear to Ibrahim, he stopped and disassociated from him, as Allah says in 9:114. And Ibn Kathir cites a narration recorded in the Sahih: on the Day of Resurrection Ibrahim will meet Āzar, who will say, "My son! This Day I will not disobey you." Ibrahim will plead, "O Lord, You promised not to disgrace me on the Day they are resurrected — and what disgrace is greater than my father being cursed?" Allah will tell him to look behind him — and he will see his father transformed into a male hyena covered in dung, seized by the legs and thrown into the Fire. The scene is sobering: even Ibrahim's pleading does not avert the consequence of dying upon shirk.

## Living the passage

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān distils two working principles from Ibrahim's method for anyone who carries truth to others:

**Match your firmness to the clarity of the error.** With idol-worship — an error obvious to anyone — Ibrahim was blunt from the first word: "manifest error." With star-worship, whose falsity was not so apparent, he never made a frontal assault; he built a gentle demonstration that let people arrive at the conclusion themselves. Neither universal rigidity nor universal leniency is right; each has its occasion and its limit.

**Testify rather than command.** Ibrahim never ordered his people to abandon their gods. He spoke only of himself — "I do not like those that set… I have turned my face…" — so that no one's pride was cornered into opposing truth merely for opposition's sake. The aim of the caller, the commentary concludes, is not simply to say what is true in any manner whatever, but to say it in the way most likely to reach the listener's heart.

Star, moon, and sun still rise and set over every reader of these ayat. The passage asks each of us what Ibrahim asked his people: will you give your love to what vanishes, or turn your face — wholly, as a ḥanīf — to the One who never sets?

passages.title: Abraham debates his people and receives the decisive argument
passages.tafsir:
# Abraham Debates His People and Receives the Decisive Argument (6:80–83)

Ibrahim (peace be upon him) has just declared, in the ayat before this passage, that he is free of everything his people associate with Allah. Now they push back. These four ayat record the counter-attack of his people, the answer that silenced them, and then — remarkably — Allah's own verdict on the debate and His disclosure of where Ibrahim's winning argument really came from. What binds the passage together is a single thread: **fear and security**. The whole exchange turns on one question — who actually has something to be afraid of, and who has the right to sleep soundly?

## The people argue back — ayah 80

"And his people argued with him." Ibn Kathir — who opens by naming Ibrahim Allah's **Khalil**, His intimate friend — explains that when Ibrahim called them to Tawhid (worshipping Allah alone), his people raised various doubts and disputes against him. His reply opens with astonishment: *"Do you dispute with me about Allah while He has guided me?"* Ibn Kathir unpacks the sense: do you argue with me about Allah, other than Whom there is no god worthy of worship, when He has guided me to the Truth and made me aware of it? How could I ever take your misguided statements and false doubts seriously after that?

The Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in what their "arguing" actually contained: a threat. They warned Ibrahim that their idols would destroy him for refusing to accept their authority. That is why his reply immediately turns to fear: *"I fear not those whom you associate with Allah — except that my Lord should will something."* Ibn Kathir draws out the challenge buried in these words: these false gods of yours produce no effect at all, so I neither fear them nor care about them — and if they really can harm, then set them loose on me and give me no respite. The exception clause, "except when my Lord wills something," is the creed in miniature: only Allah causes benefit or harm. Ibn Kathir notes how closely this mirrors the stand of Prophet Hud against his people 'Ad, who claimed "some of our gods have seized you with evil," to which Hud replied: *"So plot against me, all of you, and give me no respite. I put my trust in Allah, my Lord and your Lord"* (11:53–56). Two prophets, one posture: total fearlessness before false gods, total dependence on the true One.

Ibrahim closes the ayah with *"My Lord comprehends all things in knowledge — will you not then remember?"* — Allah's knowledge encompasses everything and nothing escapes His observation; so reflect on what I have shown you about these idols.

## Turning fear on its head — ayah 81, the decisive question

Ayah 81 is the heart of the passage — these are the very words that ayah 83 will call "Our proof," as Mujahid and others explained. Ibrahim takes their own weapon — fear — and reverses it:

**"How should I fear what you associate with Allah, while you do not fear that you have associated with Allah things for which He has sent down to you no sulṭān?"**

The word *sulṭān* here means **proof, authority** — that is the explanation of Ibn 'Abbas and others among the Salaf (the early generations), as Ibn Kathir records. Your shirk rests on nothing Allah ever revealed; it is a human invention with no warrant behind it. Ibn Kathir points to the Qur'an's parallel expressions: "partners who have instituted for them a religion which Allah has not allowed" (42:21), and "names which you have named, you and your fathers, for which Allah has sent down no authority" (53:21).

So the situation, Ibrahim says, is exactly upside-down. The Maʿārif ul Qurʼān paraphrases his answer to their threat: your idols do not have the power to destroy me, nor have I done anything to deserve hardship — in fact, it is *you* who should be trembling in fear, for you have committed a crime as terrible as equating with Allah the creations of Allah, indeed objects made by His creation, even giving them a share in His divinity. And since no sensible person can be unaware that Allah is All-Knowing, All-Aware and All-Powerful, this calls for some thinking on your part: think, and say who deserves to be at peace, and who it is who should be fearing. Then comes the question that ends the argument: *"So which of the two parties has more right to security — if you know?"* Ibn Kathir spells out the two parties: those who worship Him in Whose Hand is all harm and benefit, or those who worship what can neither harm nor benefit and have no authority for doing so — which of them deserves to be safe from Allah's punishment on the Day of Resurrection?

The Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes the psychology of this move. People worship idols, rocks, trees, rivers and stars because, in their simplicity, they take them to be wielders of power, and they are scared to abandon them lest they be hurt. Ibrahim gave such people "a smart key to their problem": fear the One who actually knows everything you do and holds all power over what reaches you — and stop fearing things that possess neither knowledge nor power. That fear is simply unreasonable. Fear Allah alone, and you are out of all danger.

## Allah Himself answers — ayah 82

Who resolves the question? On Ibn Kathir's reading, Allah does. Ibrahim posed it; ayah 82 is Allah's testimony confirming his statement and issuing the verdict:

**"Those who believe and do not mix their faith with ẓulm — for them is security, and they are the guided."**

Both halves of the question are settled at once: security (*al-amn*) in the Hereafter, and guidance (*hudā*) in this life and the next, belong to those who worship Allah alone without partners.

**The word ẓulm, and the day it frightened the Companions.** *Ẓulm* means wrong or injustice. When this ayah came down, it shook the Prophet's ﷺ Companions. Al-Bukhari recorded that 'Abdullah said: when "and confuse not their belief with ẓulm" was revealed, the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ said, "And who among us has not committed ẓulm against himself?" — until the ayah "Verily, joining others in worship with Allah is a great ẓulm indeed" (31:13) was later revealed. In the narration recorded by Imam Ahmad, they brought their distress to the Prophet ﷺ — "O Allah's Messenger! Who among us did not commit ẓulm against himself?" — and he answered: "It is not what you understood from it. Did you not hear what the righteous servant (Luqman) said: *O my son, join not in worship others with Allah; verily shirk is a great ẓulm indeed*?" So the ẓulm that cancels this promise of security is not ordinary sin — it is **shirk**, associating partners with Allah.

The Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds two precise language notes. *Lam yalbisū* ("have not mixed") comes from *labasa*, to wear, cover, or mix — faith contaminated, clothed over, by something foreign to it. And *bi-ẓulmin* is grammatically indefinite (a *nakirah*, "any ẓulm"), which by the rules of Arabic generalises the sense: the promise excludes **every kind** of shirk, not only its crudest forms. From this the Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a sobering application: shirk is not restricted to the temple idolater. A person may recite the Kalimah of Islam — the statement of faith — and still fall into shirk by assigning to an angel, a messenger, a *walī* or "saint" of Allah a share in attributes that belong exclusively to Him. The verse, it says, carries a stern warning for those who treat the Awliyāʼ of Allah (the Men of Allah) and their tombs as capable of answering prayers and granting needs, as though Divine powers had been delegated to them — refuge with Allah!

## "That was Our proof" — ayah 83

Then Allah lifts the curtain: *"And that was Our proof which We gave Ibrahim against his people."* The brilliant argument was not Ibrahim's cleverness; it was a gift. Ibn Kathir cites Mujahid and others that "Our proof" refers specifically to the argument of ayah 81 — "How should I fear what you associate… so which of the two parties has more right to security?" That reversal of fear, the question no honest polytheist could answer, was authored by Allah, Who directed Ibrahim to proclaim it against them.

The Maʿārif ul Qurʼān dwells on the lesson: Ibrahim's triumph in this debate was a blessing of Allah alone, for it was He who gave him a sound theory to propound and glowing arguments to employ. Let no one grow proud of his intelligence, his understanding, or his power of speech as if these were self-sufficient. Bare human reason is not enough to grasp realities — philosophers of great standing go astray while many of the unlettered take firm hold of correct belief. Victory in argument, like guidance itself, is Allah's blessing.

*"We raise in degrees whom We will."* The Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads in this a hint at the station Ibrahim was granted: a reverence lasting through every generation until the Last Day, a homage paid to him across faiths — and none of it a personal acquisition; all of it grace and reward from Allah.

The passage seals with two of Allah's names: *"Certainly your Lord is All-Wise, All-Knowing."* Ibn Kathir explains: All-Wise in His statements and actions, All-Knowing of those whom He guides or misguides, and of whether the proof was established against them or not — for as Allah says elsewhere, those against whom His Word has been justified will not believe "even if every sign should come to them, until they see the painful torment" (10:96–97).

## Living it

Two things this passage asks of a believer, both drawn directly from the commentary. First, **relocate your fear**. Whatever people around you treat as holding power over harm and benefit — the ayah's logic strips it bare. Only Allah causes benefit or harm; the one who fears Him alone, as the Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, is "out of all danger." Second, **guard the purity of your Tawhid**. The Companions' alarm at this ayah, and the Prophet's ﷺ correction, teach that the promise of security is real and its condition is specific: faith unmixed with shirk of any kind — including the subtle kinds that dress themselves in religious clothing. And when you do find yourself defending the truth well, remember ayah 83: the argument, like the guidance, was given.

passages.title: The chain of prophets Abraham's line inherited
passages.tafsir:
This passage is a roll-call of the prophetic family. Allah here displays what He gave Ibrahim in return for his sacrifice: a chain of seventeen prophets — forefathers, sons, grandsons, brothers and nephews of his house — each one guided, chosen, and set upon a straight path. What binds ayat 84–90 into one unit is a single running idea: guidance is Allah's gift, given to one family line as the reward for one man's sacrifice — and the passage closes by turning to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ with the command that he, and through him this Ummah, walk the very path that family walked.

## The gift that answered a sacrifice

Ayah 84 opens with a word of pure grace: *wa-wahabnā* — "And We **bestowed** upon him Ishaq and Ya'qub." Ibn Kathir sets the scene: Ibrahim had grown old, and he and his wife Sarah had lost all hope of children, when the angels — passing on their way to the people of Lut — delivered the good news. Sarah was astonished: "Shall I bear a child while I am an old woman, and here is my husband, an old man?" (as recounted in 11:72–73). The news came doubled: not only a son, Ishaq, who would himself be a prophet, but a grandson after him, Ya'qub — whose very name, Ibn Kathir notes, literally means "multiplying and having offspring." An elderly couple's child might be expected to leave no line at all; instead Ibrahim was promised a lineage he would see with his own eyes, "so that his eyes would be comforted."

Why this gift? Both commentaries insist on the connection: **this was a reward for what Ibrahim gave up.** He left his people and migrated from their land so that he could worship Allah alone, and Allah "compensated Ibrahim with better than his people and tribe" (Ibn Kathir). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān spells the exchange out item by item: he left his father and mother, his people and country for Allah's sake — and became the patriarch of the prophets. He abandoned the greenery of Syria for the deserts of Makkah to raise the foundations of the House of Allah — and was blessed with Baytullah (the House of Allah), al-Balad al-Amin (the City of Trust) and Umm al-Qura (the Mother of Cities), Makkah al-Mukarramah. He obeyed instantly when told to leave his wife and infant son in the wilderness, and showed complete readiness when commanded to sacrifice his dear son. His own people tried to disgrace him — and he was made a leader whom nations and religions, despite all their differences, have remained united in revering until the Last Day.

From this Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a general law: **whoever sacrifices what he holds dear in the way of Allah is given, right here in this world — before the reward of the Hereafter — something better than what he surrendered.** The real reward of such obedience comes only in Jannah; but Allah does not make His servants wait empty-handed.

## Seventeen prophets, one household

Ayat 84–86 then unfold the list: Nuh before him; and among the progeny — Dawud, Sulayman, Ayyub, Yusuf, Musa and Harun (ayah 84); Zakariyya, Yahya, 'Isa and Ilyas, "each one of them was of the righteous" (ayah 85); Isma'il, al-Yasa', Yunus and Lut, "each one of them We preferred above the 'ālamīn" — above the worlds, which Ibn Kathir's rendering glosses as mankind and jinn *of their times* (ayah 86). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān counts seventeen blessed prophets across verses 84–89.

Ibn Kathir pauses on the special quality of the two patriarchs who frame the list. After the Flood, every human being on earth has descended from **Nuh**. And after **Ibrahim**, Allah never sent a prophet except from his descendants — as other ayat state, "We ordained among his offspring prophethood and the Book" (29:27; likewise 57:26). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces the two great branches: from **Ishaq** came the prophets of the Bani Isra'il; from **Isma'il** came the foremost and last of the prophets, Muhammad al-Mustafa ﷺ. Every later messenger, to the end of time, was Ibrahim's own progeny — the supreme distinction, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls it.

Notice the refrain that closes ayah 84: "Thus do We reward the good-doers." It carries the point both commentaries make: this family line was itself the reward for Ibrahim's sacrifice.

## Two puzzles in the family tree

The classical scholars noticed two names that do not fit a strict father-to-son reading of "his progeny," and both commentaries address them.

**First, 'Isa.** He had no father at all, and connects to Ibrahim only through his mother Maryam. Yet the ayah counts him in the progeny. Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān both draw the conclusion: **grandchildren through a daughter are truly one's offspring.** Ibn Abi Hatim recorded the famous exchange: al-Hajjaj sent to Yahya bin Ya'mar, saying, "I was told that you claim that al-Hasan and al-Husayn are from the offspring of the Prophet ﷺ. Did you find it in the Book of Allah? I read the Qur'an from beginning to end and did not find it." Yahya answered from this very passage: is not 'Isa from the offspring of Ibrahim, although he did not have a father? Al-Hajjaj could only concede: "You have said the truth." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that most learned Muslim scholars and jurists prove from this very ayah that al-Hasan and al-Husayn, the sons of the Prophet's ﷺ daughter, stand included in his progeny. Ibn Kathir even draws a practical legal note from it: a legacy, trust or gift made to one's "offspring" includes the children of daughters, whereas one made to one's "sons" is particular to the male line.

**Second, Lut.** He was not Ibrahim's child but his nephew — the son of his brother, as Ibn Kathir records. He is included by a generous breadth in family speech: just as the Qur'an has Ya'qub's sons name Isma'il among their father's "fathers" (2:133) though he was Ya'qub's uncle, and just as Iblis was included in the command given to the angels though he was of the jinn (15:30–31), the nephew is folded into the household. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds simply that calling a nephew a son is very common in customary usage. (Ibn Kathir also records another possibility, from Ibn Jarir: the pronoun in "among *his* progeny" may refer back to Nuh rather than Ibrahim — a genuine difference among the commentators, and he leaves both readings open.)

Ayah 87 then widens the circle beyond the seventeen: "And also some of their fathers and their progeny and their brethren — We chose them, and We guided them to a straight path." Guidance flowed upward, downward and sideways through this family. Yet Maʿārif ul Qurʼān enters a careful caution here: honour and salvation, or disgrace and punishment, **really depend on one's personal deeds**. Having a prophet or a walī (a devoted friend of Allah) among one's forefathers, or righteous scholars and people of good conduct among one's children, is a great blessing that brings real benefit — but it is a blessing, not a substitute for one's own faith and works.

## Even prophets' deeds would perish through shirk

Ayah 88 names the source of it all: "This is the guidance of Allah, with which He guides whomsoever He wills of His servants." Their greatness, Ibn Kathir says, occurred by Allah's leave and because He directed them — it was never self-made.

Then comes the thunderclap: "But if they had associated others with Allah, all that they used to do would have been of no benefit to them." If even *these* — seventeen prophets — had committed shirk (associating partners with Allah in worship), every deed of theirs would have collapsed. This, Ibn Kathir says, magnifies the serious danger of shirk and the gravity of committing it, and he pairs it with 39:65: "If you join others in worship with Allah, surely your deeds will be in vain." He is equally careful about what the ayah does *not* mean: the "if" here does not mean that this would ever occur — it is of the same kind as "Say: if the Most Beneficent had a son, then I am the first of worshippers" (43:81).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān shows how this lands on the first audience. The disbelievers of Makkah are, in effect, told: consider these whom you too revere as great — Ibrahim and his whole progeny have all been saying one thing, that Allah alone is worthy of worship, and that giving anyone a share in His worship or His exclusive attributes is disbelief and straying. By the very truths the Makkans themselves accepted, their idolatry stood condemned.

## The trust never falls to the ground

Ayah 89 gathers the whole line into one description: "They are those whom We gave the Book, al-Hukm, and prophethood" — bounties bestowed, Ibn Kathir says, "as a mercy for the servants" and out of kindness for creation.

"But if they disbelieve therein" — in the prophethood, Ibn Kathir explains, or in all three things, the Book, the Hukm and the prophethood — the "they" here, according to Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id bin al-Musayyib, ad-Dahhak, Qatadah, as-Suddi and others, are the people of Makkah — "then indeed We have entrusted it to a people who are not disbelievers therein." Ibn Kathir identifies that people: the Muhajirun and the Ansar, **and those who follow their lead until the Day of Resurrection.** They will not deny these favours "not even one letter"; they believe even in the parts that are not so clear to some of them. And he closes with his own plea: "We ask Allah to make us among them by His favor, generosity and kindness."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the ayah as comfort addressed to the Prophet ﷺ: if some of your hearers are bent on nothing short of denial, do not worry — Allah has appointed a great people who will say yes to your call, follow your word and make the mission their own. And it calls this verse "a fond asset" for every Muslim to the end of time, for Allah has named them here on an occasion of praise — then records the fitting response: *Allāhumma ijʿalnā minhum wa-ḥshurnā fī zumratihim* — "O Allah, make us one of them and raise us in their company."

## "So follow their guidance"

Ayah 90 is the destination of the whole list: "They are those whom Allah had guided — **so follow their guidance**." The command is addressed to the Messenger ﷺ, and, as Ibn Kathir says, it certainly applies to his Ummah according to what he legislates and commands.

Al-Bukhari recorded that Mujahid asked Ibn 'Abbas whether there is an instance where prostration is warranted in Surah Sad. Ibn 'Abbas said yes — and then recited from "And We bestowed upon him Ishaq and Ya'qub" up to "so follow their guidance," and commented, "He — our Prophet, Muhammad ﷺ — was among them." In another narration, Ibn 'Abbas said, "Your Prophet ﷺ was among those whose guidance we were commanded to follow."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls the guidance of this verse "bi-polar" — it cuts in two directions at once. **To the people of Arabia** (and by implication the whole Muslim Ummah): forefathers are not automatically role-models. The people of Arabia, and of Makkah particularly, followed their forefathers to the letter in all their words and deeds simply because they were forefathers; the ayah teaches that before following anyone, one must first ask whether that person is himself on the path of true guidance. It is *"those whom Allah has guided"* whose guidance is to be followed. **To the Prophet ﷺ himself**: he too is to act as the guided prophets before him acted.

But the laws of the earlier prophets differed in their details — so what does "follow their guidance" mean? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers, in view of other Qur'anic verses and narrations of hadith: the command concerns not the subsidiary rulings, which changed with the exigency of time and the dictate of wisdom, but **the basic principles of religion — Tawhid (the Oneness of Allah), Risalah (prophethood), and Akhirah (the Hereafter)** — which never changed in the law of any prophet. From Adam to the Last of the Prophets ﷺ, all of them held one Belief and one Way. Indeed, it was the Prophet's ﷺ usual practice to act in accordance with the way of the past prophets until particular guidance came to him through revelation (as Mazhari and others note).

The passage closes with the command to proclaim: "Say: No reward do I ask of you for this. It is only a reminder for the worlds." I gain nothing if you accept, I lose nothing if you refuse; this is good counsel offered free — no fees, no wages, no rewards. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that not accepting any return for teaching and preaching has been the common legacy of all the prophets, and a powerful factor in making *tabligh* (conveying the message of religion to others) effective. And the Qur'an itself, Ibn Kathir concludes, is that reminder: by it people are led from blindness to clarity, from misguidance to guidance, and from disbelief to faith.

## Living this passage

Four threads to carry away. Salvation rests on your own deeds — yet a righteous ancestor or a righteous child is a real blessing that brings real benefit, so treasure both. Whatever you genuinely give up for Allah's sake, expect His law of compensation: something better, in this world before the next. Never follow anyone — ancestor, culture, or authority — until you have asked whether they themselves are guided. And when you convey this religion, convey it as the prophets did: seeking no return from anyone, for that has been their common legacy.

passages.title: They fail to honour Allah and His revelation
passages.tafsir:
This passage is about the two opposite ways people fail to honour Allah's revelation: denying that He ever sent any (ayah 91), and forging revelation of their own (ayah 93). Between these two crimes stands the genuine article — the blessed Qur'an (ayah 92) — and after them comes the reckoning: the agony of the soul's exit at death, and the solitary return to Allah with empty hands (ayat 93–94). What binds the four ayat together is the opening charge: *wa-mā qadarū Allāha ḥaqqa qadrihi* — "they have not shown Allah His proper reverence." Whoever truly takes Allah's measure will neither deny His Books nor counterfeit them; whoever belittles Him will end up doing one or the other.

## "They did not estimate Allah as is His due" (ayah 91)

The ayah opens with a striking phrase: they did not *estimate* Allah with the estimation due to Him. Ibn Kathir explains that those who rejected Allah's Messengers "did not give Allah due consideration," and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unfolds the logic: had these people truly recognised Allah as He deserves to be recognised, "this audacious remark would have never escaped their lips." The remark in question was breathtaking in its sweep — "Nothing did Allah send down to any human being." Not a rejection of one prophet or one book, but of the very idea that Allah communicates with mankind at all.

**Who said it?** The early authorities differed. Ibn Kathir reports from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and 'Abdullah bin Kathir that the ayah was revealed about the Quraysh — and he connects it to their recurring astonishment, quoted elsewhere in the Qur'an, that Allah would send *a man* as Messenger (10:2, 17:94–95). Others said it was revealed about some of the Jews, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the contextual elements of the verse support this view — for the verse goes on to address people who possess the Torah. If a Jew said it, Maʿārif observes, it was an outburst of anger and irritation that contradicted his own religion. Indeed, according to a narration of Imam al-Baghawi, the Jews themselves were displeased with the man who made this unfortunate remark, and because of it he was removed from his office of religious authority. The two views need not trouble the reader: the ayah's argument cuts against every denier of revelation, Makkan idolater and angry scriptuary alike.

**The unanswerable question.** Allah instructs His Prophet ﷺ to reply with a single question: "Who then sent down the Book which Musa brought, a light and a guidance to mankind?" The Torah's existence was not in dispute — the very people making the denial believed in it, and, as Maʿārif puts it, sat in judgment over their people on its authority. Ibn Kathir notes that Allah sent the Torah "as a light and a guidance for people, so that it could shed light on the answers to various disputes, and to guide away from the darkness of doubts." So the denial refutes itself: if no human being ever received revelation, where did the Torah come from? 'Ali bin Abi Talhah reported that Ibn 'Abbas explained the ayah's terse reply — *qul Allāh* — as: "Say, Allah sent it down." The question admits no other answer.

**The Torah on loose sheets.** But the ayah presses further, exposing *how* these people handled the Book they professed to honour: "which you have made into separate papersheets, disclosing some of it and concealing much." The word *qarāṭīs* is the plural of *qirṭās*, a sheet of paper. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the accusation: they deliberately kept the Torah on loose, unbound sheets rather than as a formally bound book — so that any sheet could be quietly removed when its contents proved inconvenient, giving them "the option of denying what it enjoined." The prime example, Maʿārif says, were the verses of the Torah describing the signs and attributes of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, which they excluded. Ibn Kathir adds the darker half of the crime: they copied from the original, "altered, changed and distorted as you wished," and then said "this is from Allah" — when in fact it was not from Allah. Loose sheets are the perfect instrument for a religion of convenience: display what suits you, conceal what indicts you.

Then comes a gift wrapped inside the rebuke: "And you were taught that which neither you nor your fathers knew" — the Qur'an, in which Allah taught them news of those before them and of what is to come, knowledge that neither the Torah nor the Injil had given them. And finally, dismissal: "Then leave them to play in their vain discussions." Maʿārif explains the sense: once the argument against them stands concluded, the Prophet's ﷺ mission toward them is discharged — let them be lost in their game. Ibn Kathir adds: leave them to play in ignorance until the true news comes to them from Allah, and then they will know whose end is good.

## The blessed Book and the Mother of Towns (ayah 92)

Having silenced the deniers, the passage turns to the Book they were really trying to escape: "And this is a blessed Book which We have sent down, confirming what came before it." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the elegance of the argument: since they accept that the Torah came down from Allah, here is the Qur'an — and sufficient proof of its truth is that it *confirms* what was revealed in the Torah and the Injil rather than contradicting it.

**Why after the Torah and Injil?** Maʿārif answers: those two Books were sent for the Bani Isra'il, while their other branch, the Bani Isma'il — the Arabs living in Makkah and its environs — had received no prophet and no book of guidance until that time. Now the Qur'an has come: for them particularly, and for the whole world generally.

**Umm al-Qura.** The Qur'an calls Makkah "the Mother of Towns" — the root and foundation of all towns and habitations. Maʿārif (citing Mazhari) gives two reasons: according to historical narratives, the land mass of the earth first began appearing from there; and it is the Qiblah, the central attraction of all acts of worship for the whole world. And the phrase "and all those around it" is not a local reference — it means the whole world east, west, north and south of Makkah. Ibn Kathir strings together the parallel ayat that make the universality explicit — "Say: O mankind! Verily, I am sent to you all as the Messenger of Allah" (7:158), "that I may therewith warn you and whomsoever it may reach" (6:19) — and cites the hadith recorded in the Two Sahihs in which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "I have been given five things which were not given to anyone else before me," among them: "Every Prophet was sent only to his nation, but I have been sent to all people."

**The mark of true believers.** The ayah closes with a signature: "Those who believe in the Hereafter believe in it, and they are constant in guarding their Salah." Ibn Kathir explains: those who believe in Allah and the Last Day believe in this Book, and they offer the prayers perfectly and on time. Maʿārif sees in this a pointed admonition. The common ailment of the Book's opponents was pick-and-choose religion — accepting what they liked and rejecting what they did not — and the root of that ailment is weak belief in the *Akhirah*, the Hereafter. Whoever genuinely believes that a Day of Judgment is coming will be moved by the fear of Allah to reason honestly, and once convinced, will bypass the constraints of ignorant custom and embrace the truth. Maʿārif presses the point further: lack of concern for the Akhirah is "the mother of all spiritual diseases" — from it come disbelief, associating partners with Allah, sin and disobedience. A believer in the Akhirah who slips into sin feels the pinch in his heart, repents, and resolves to stay away. This is why, Maʿārif observes, hardly a surah of the Qur'an — perhaps hardly a section — passes without a reminder of the Hereafter. He closes with a prayer: *O Allah, make all our concerns a single concern — the concern for the Akhirah.*

## The opposite crime: forging revelation (ayah 93)

Ayah 91 dealt with those who deny that Allah reveals anything. Ayah 93 turns to their mirror image: those who claim revelation falsely. "Who does more wrong than the one who fabricates lies against Allah, or says: 'I have received inspiration,' whereas he is not inspired with anything?" Ibn Kathir spells out the scope: none is more unjust than one who lies about Allah — claiming He has partners or a son — or who falsely claims that Allah sent him as a Prophet. 'Ikrimah and Qatadah said this ayah was revealed about Musaylimah al-Kadhdhab. The ayah adds a third figure: the one who says, "I will reveal the like of what Allah has revealed" — the boaster, Ibn Kathir explains, who claims his invented words rival Allah's revelation, like those who said of the Qur'an, "if we wish we can say the like of this."

Notice the architecture of the passage: the denier says revelation comes to *no one*; the forger says it comes to *him*. Both are lies against Allah, and both flow from the same failure to take His true measure.

**The agonies of death.** Then the ayah lifts the veil on where such lies end: "If you could but see when the wrongdoers are in the agonies of death, while the angels are stretching forth their hands: 'Deliver your souls!'" Ibn Kathir describes the scene with terrible vividness. The wrongdoers suffer the hardships and afflictions of death while the angels stretch forth their hands — meaning, as ad-Dahhak and Abu Salih explained, *with torment* — beating them, as in the parallel ayah, "the angels take away the souls of those who disbelieve, smiting their faces and their backs" (8:50). When the disbeliever nears death, the angels convey to him the "good news" of torment, vengeance, chains, Hell, boiling water and the anger of the Most Beneficent, Most Merciful — and the soul, hearing it, scatters through the body and refuses to come out. The angels keep striking until it exits, saying: "Deliver your souls! This day you shall be recompensed with the torment of degradation because of what you used to say about Allah other than the truth." The humiliation fits the crime precisely: they exalted themselves with lies against Allah and arrogantly rejected His ayat, so they are brought out of the world in utter disgrace. Ibn Kathir notes that many hadiths of *mutawatir* grade — transmitted through so many channels that their authenticity is beyond doubt — describe what happens to believers and disbelievers at death, and he defers their full presentation to his commentary on 14:27.

## Alone, as you were created (ayah 94)

The final ayah is the address they will hear on the Day of Return: "You have come back to Us all alone, as We created you the first time." Ibn Kathir pairs it with 18:48 — "Now indeed, you have come to Us as We created you the first time" — and draws out the irony: just as Allah began your creation, He has brought you back, though you used to deny resurrection and reject its possibility. The Day itself is the refutation.

Three things are stripped away in this ayah, one by one:

**Wealth.** "You have left behind you all that which We had bestowed on you." Every coin gathered in the world stays in the world. Ibn Kathir cites the hadith recorded in the Sahih: "The Son of Adam says, 'My money, my money!' But what part of your money do you have, other than what you eat and thus spend, what you wear and tear, and what you give in charity — which remains? Everything else you will depart from and leave to the people." Al-Hasan al-Basri, in a statement recorded by Ibn Abi Hatim, pictured the scene: the Son of Adam is brought forward, and Allah asks, "Where is what you collected?" He answers, "O Lord, I collected it and left it as intact as ever." Allah says, "O Son of Adam! Where is what you sent forth *for yourself*?" — and he realises he sent forth nothing.

**Intercessors.** "We see not with you your intercessors whom you claimed to be your partners." Ibn Kathir explains that this chastises the disbelievers over the idols and rivals they worshipped, imagining these would avail them — "partners," he notes pointedly, "in a share of your worship." On that Day, Allah will call out while all creation listens: "Where are My so-called partners whom you used to assert?" (28:62) — and the invented gods will simply have vanished.

**Ties.** "Now you and they have been cut off" — or, on another recitation of the ayah, as Ibn Kathir records, *all connections, means, and ties between you have been severed*. He gathers the parallel ayat: leaders will disown followers (2:166–167), kinship will count for nothing when the Trumpet is blown (23:101), and the idol-based friendships of this world will turn to mutual cursing (29:25). "And all that you used to claim has vanished from you."

## Living it

The passage begins with people who would not give Allah His true measure and ends with a human being standing alone before Him, stripped of money, intercessors and allies. Between those two points, it asks something concrete of the believer. Take the whole Book, not loose sheets of it — the pick-and-choose religion of the *qarāṭīs* is condemned precisely because it displays what suits and conceals what indicts. Receive the Qur'an as what ayah 92 declares it to be: blessed, confirming what came before, sent for all the world. And cultivate the two marks that ayah gives of those who truly believe: living belief in the Hereafter, and guarding the prayer — performed properly and on time. For as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān teaches, concern for the Akhirah is the root that keeps every other branch of the religion alive; and ayah 94 shows why: the return journey is made alone, and only what was sent ahead will be waiting.

passages.title: Signs of the Creator in seed, dawn, and rain
passages.tafsir:
# Signs of the Creator in Seed, Dawn, and Rain (6:95–99)

This passage is Sūrat al-Anʿām's great gallery of creation. The verses before it exposed how obstinately the disbelievers and polytheists clung to falsehood; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that these verses now supply the antidote. Such delusion grows out of unawareness of Allah and His unmatched knowledge and power — so Allah lays out samples of that power, each one something the listener depends on daily but could never produce: the sprouting seed, the breaking dawn, the night of rest, the clockwork sun and moon, the guiding stars, a whole human race from one soul, and the rain that turns dry wood into dates and grapes. One refrain holds it all together: everything here points back to its Maker — *\"Such is Allah; how then are you deluded away from the truth?\"* (ayah 95).

## The Splitter of seed and stone (ayah 95)

The key word is **fāliq** — \"the one who splits.\" The Qurʼān uses it twice in this passage: Allah is the splitter of *al-ḥabb wa'l-nawā*, the grain and the fruit-stone (ayah 95), and the splitter of *al-iṣbāḥ*, the daybreak (ayah 96). The same word covers germination and dawn — two daily cleavings, one in the soil and one in the sky.

Ibn Kathir says the opening phrase is explained by the clause that follows it: \"He brings forth the living from the dead\" means He brings a living green plant out of a lifeless, inanimate seed or stone — producing grains and produce of every type, colour, shape and taste. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses the point with the farmer: everything a farmer does — ploughing, cleaning, softening, levelling, fertilizing, watering — only clears obstacles from the seedling's path. The real work, the splitting of the seed, the rising shoot, the leaves of many wonderful kinds and colours, the flowers and fruits of astonishing variety, is done by Someone else; no human ingenuity can come close to making so much as one leaf or one petal that way. It cites Allah's challenge elsewhere: *\"Do you see the seed that you sow? Do you make it grow, or are We the One who makes it grow?\"* (56:63–64).

\"The living from the dead\" then widens. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān applies it to the lifeless cell or egg which serves to create human and animal life; Ibn Kathir mentions the egg from the chicken and the chicken from the egg, and relates that others read it morally — the wicked offspring from the righteous parent, and the reverse — noting the ayah carries other possible meanings as well.

Then comes the turn the whole passage exists for: *dhālikum Allāh* — \"the One who does all this is Allah, the One and Only without partners\" (Ibn Kathir). *Fa-annā tuʾfakūn* — how are you turned from this plain truth to the falsehood of taking self-carved idols, in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's words, as your \"removers of difficulties and fulfillers of needs\"?

## Dawn for work, night for rest (ayah 96)

**Fāliq al-iṣbāḥ**: He tears the dark layer of darkness apart and brings the morning out of it (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān). Ibn Kathir reads it with its opposite: He is the Creator of both light and darkness — the very note this sūrah opened on: *\"and originated the darkness and the light\"* (6:1).

**Sakan** — \"He has made the night a *sakan*\" — comes from *sukūn*, stillness: anything, a time or a place, by having or reaching which one feels peaceful and comfortable is a sakan, which is why the Qurʼān calls your home a sakan (16:80). The night is a home you enter every day.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān dwells on what a mercy this is precisely because it arrives unasked. Imagine if every person fixed their own hours of rest — one sleeping at eight in the morning, another at noon, factories and traffic running through all twenty-four hours; the noise of the working would ruin the sleep of the resting, and the absence of the sleeping would hobble the working. And even if all governments signed a universal agreement on sleeping hours, who would make the animals abide by it? Instead, Allah has appointed sleep to descend upon every human being and every living creature at a given time compulsively — with the fall of dusk, birds and beasts and cattle head for their nests and homes, silence reigns, and darkness itself becomes sleep's ally. *\"So, blessed be Allah, the Best of creators\"* (23:14).

**Ḥusbān** — the sun and moon \"for reckoning\" — means to count, measure, calculate or compute. Their risings, settings and movements are set to a particular measure by which humans can easily calculate years, months, days, hours, even minutes and seconds. Ibn Kathir: they have specific orbits, appointed with magnificent precision that never changes or alters, taking distinct positions in summer and winter that change the very length of night and day — *\"It is not for the sun to overtake the moon, nor does the night outstrip the day\"* (36:40). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a piercing irony: it was the very flawlessness of this machinery — never breaking down, never needing repair or replacement of parts — that deceived people into taking the sun and moon as existing in their own right, even worshipping them. Had the system been open to flaws, a little malfunction here and there, they would have discovered that somebody made it and somebody keeps it running. It was to let them know this that scriptures, prophets and messengers were sent.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also draws a practical ruling from *ḥusbān*: both solar and lunar reckoning are rewards from Allah, but Islamic injunctions were tied to the lunar calendar for the convenience of the common masses, so the Muslim Ummah is obliged to retain and protect it. Adopting a solar calendar out of some necessity is no sin — but ignoring the lunar calendar totally, until a Muslim no longer knows when Ramadan, Dhul-Hijjah or Muharram falls, is a grave sin.

The verse seals itself: *\"Such is the measuring of al-ʿAzīz, al-ʿAlīm\"* — the Almighty whose decree is never resisted or contradicted, the All-Knowing from whose knowledge nothing ever escapes, not even the weight of an atom on earth or in the heavens (Ibn Kathir). Ibn Kathir observes that Allah often mentions the creation of the night, the day, the sun and the moon and then ends His Speech with exactly this pair of attributes — power and knowledge — as in 36:37–38 and 41:12.

## Stars to steer by (ayah 97)

The stars are \"set for you, so that you may guide your course with their help through the darkness of the land and the sea.\" Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that experience bears this out even in the days of highly sophisticated guiding systems: there remain situations where guidance from the position of the stars cannot be totally ignored.

Ibn Kathir relates that some of the Salaf (the early generations) said: whoever believes anything about these stars beyond three things has made a mistake and lied against Allah — Allah made them as decorations for the heavens, to shoot at the shayāṭīn (the devils), and for directions in the dark recesses of the land and sea. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the deeper point: the stars themselves are observing the command of their Maker and Mover; they are neither there by themselves nor doing what they do forever. Whoever pins his sights on them while ignoring the One behind them is terribly short-sighted, and ominously deceived indeed.

## One soul, a dwelling and a lodging (ayah 98)

\"He originated you all from a single soul\" — from Adam, peace be upon him (Ibn Kathir, citing 4:1). Then come two dense words. **Mustaqarr**, from *qarār*, is a place of rest and peace. **Mustawdaʿ** derives from a word meaning to keep something with someone temporarily for a few days — so it denotes a place where a thing is placed only temporarily (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān).

Where are these two stations? The commentators differed, and there is room for all of it within the words of the Qurʼān. Ibn Kathir reports from Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Qatādah, as-Suddī and many others that the *mustaqarr* is in the wombs — and they, or most of them, also said the *mustawdaʿ* is in the father's loins; and from Ibn Masʿūd and several others, that the *mustaqarr* is residence in this life and the *mustawdaʿ* the place of storage after death, the grave. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the further view of Qāḍī Thanāʼullāh Pānīpatī in his Tafsīr Maẓharī: the only true *mustaqarr* — settled home — is the abode of the Ākhirah, Jannah or Jahannam; everything before it — the womb, a dwelling on the earth, the grave, the state of barzakh (the intermediary state after death and before the Resurrection) — is all *mustawdaʿ*, temporary lodging. He finds confirmation in the ayah *\"you shall surely travel from stage to stage\"* (84:19).

On that reading the verse becomes, in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's phrase, a mirror held up to anyone who has sold his soul to the veneer of glamour he sees in the world: man remains a traveller his whole life who, despite his obvious peace and rest, is really traversing the stages of a long journey toward his Creator and the ultimate domain of the Ākhirah. The message: open your eyes, see reality, walk away from the web of deception and walk into salvation.

## Rain, and the taste of the harvest (ayah 99)

Now the passage follows the water down.
