Ibn Kathir points out that before revelation they themselves used to call him al-Amin — the Truthful — and that when Heraclius, emperor of Rome, questioned Abu Sufyan, the leader of the Quraysh disbelievers had to admit, "His ancestry is highly regarded among us," and, asked whether the Prophet ﷺ had ever lied before his mission, answered "No." Ibn Kathir cites the hadith recorded by Imam Ahmad from Wathilah bin al-Asqaʿ — a hadith Muslim recorded — that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Verily, Allah has chosen Isma'il from the offspring of Ibrahim, Bani Kinanah from the offspring of Isma'il, Quraysh from Bani Kinanah, Bani Hashim from Quraysh and, He has chosen me from Bani Hashim." And al-Bukhari recorded from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I was chosen from a succession of the best generations of the Children of Adam, until the generation I was sent in."

The ayah ends with a threat matched precisely to the crime: *ṣaghār* — a word Maʿārif notes is a verbal noun meaning disgrace — and a severe torment "for that which they used to plot." These antagonists of truth, known as the big chiefs of their people, will see their pride and prestige rolling in dust. Ibn Kathir observes the fitting justice: they were arrogant in this world, so it is befitting that they earn disgrace on the Day of Resurrection; and since plotting happens in secret, it will be dragged into the open — "The Day when all the secrets will be examined" (86:9). In the Two Sahihs it is recorded that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "A banner will be raised for every deceitful person from his anus on the Day of Resurrection, and it will say: 'This is the treacherous plot of so-and-so, son of so-and-so, son of so-and-so.'" The wisdom, Ibn Kathir explains, is that a plot hatched in secret will on that Day become public news, testifying against its maker. Maʿārif adds that the disgrace can come in this world too: the boastful chiefs of Quraysh either entered Islam or, like Abu Jahl and Abu Lahab, were destroyed in disgrace, their backs broken by the Conquest of Makkah.

## The opened heart and the constricted heart (ayah 125)

Now the passage moves from the outer drama to its hidden root: "Whomsoever Allah wills to guide, He opens his breast to Islam; and whomsoever He wills to send astray, He makes his breast closed and constricted, as if he is climbing up to the sky."

*Sharḥ aṣ-ṣadr* — the "opening of the breast" — means, says Ibn Kathir, that Allah makes Islam easy for the person and strengthens his resolve to embrace it; Ibn ʿAbbas said Allah opens his heart to Tawhid (affirming the oneness of Allah) and faith in Him — a comment Ibn Kathir notes was also reported from Abu Malik and several others, and is sound. The opposite state is a heart "closed and constricted," unable to accept guidance "because of the heaviness of faith on him": Saʿid bin Jubayr said that Islam "finds every path in his heart impassable."

Then comes one of the Qur'an's most striking similes. Why is the refuser "as if he is climbing up to the sky"? Al-Hakam bin Aban related that ʿIkrimah narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas: "Just as the Son of Adam cannot climb up to the sky, Tawhid and faith will not be able to enter his heart, until Allah decides to allow it into his heart." Imam Abu Jaʿfar bin Jarir put it as a parable of sheer incapacity: accepting faith becomes, for such a heart, as far beyond its power as scaling the heavens. The ayah states plainly that guidance and misguidance follow Allah's will — the same will that Ibn Kathir, at ayah 122, described as decreeing "out of His wisdom."

The closing phrase reads: "Thus Allah puts the *rijs* on those who believe not" — *rijs* being rendered "wrath" in the translation Ibn Kathir comments on. On its precise sense the early authorities differed, and Ibn Kathir records the views side by side: Ibn ʿAbbas (as ʿAli bin Abi Talhah reported from him) said *rijs* is Shaytan; Mujahid said it is everything containing no goodness; and ʿAbdur-Rahman bin Zayd bin Aslam said it is torment. Ibn Jarir added that just as Allah makes the heart of the one He misguides closed and constricted, He also appoints Shaytan for him and his likes, who lures and hinders them from the path of Allah.

Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān brings the ayah's own commentary from the Prophet ﷺ. Hakim in al-Mustadrak and Baihaqi in Shuʿab al-Iman report from ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿud that when this ayah was revealed, the Companions asked what the opening of the breast is. He said: Allah puts a light in the believer's heart through which it opens up for the perception, understanding and acceptance of truth. Is there a sign by which such a person is known? "Yes! The sign is that 'Akhirah and its blessings become the object of all his desires. He avoids uncalled-for desires and fleeting enjoyments and starts getting ready for death before it comes." The constricted heart has its sign too: Ibn ʿAbbas said that when such a person "hears the Dhikr of Allah, he feels being harassed and when he listens to what is Kufr and Shirk, his heart relishes it."

Maʿārif adds a practical observation for an age of doubts: the Companions, whose hearts were opened, asked remarkably few questions — their hearts had become in themselves the very standard of truth. Doubts are not untangled by endless debate (the philosopher deep in debate, as the poet Akbar Ilahabadi put it, never finds his way to Allah) but by thinking of the perfect power of Allah and His blessings until love and reverence fill the heart — which is why the Qur'an itself prompted the Prophet ﷺ to make the duʿā: *Rabbi-shraḥ lī ṣadrī* — "O my Rabb, open my heart."

## "The path of your Lord" — and why "straight" is not merely an adjective (ayah 126)

"And this is the path of your Lord leading straight." Ibn Masʿud said "this" refers to the Qur'an; Ibn ʿAbbas said it means Islam — the same pair of answers Ibn Kathir recorded for the "light" of ayah 122, where he judged both meanings correct.

Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān lingers lovingly over the wording. The path is attributed to *ar-Rabb* — the Sustainer and Nurturer — signalling that this Way was laid down not for Allah's benefit but for the nurturing of those who walk it, guaranteeing their eternal well-being. And it is *rabbika*, "**your** Lord," addressed to the Prophet ﷺ — the impression of a special kindness, as if the Lord of all were saying "I am yours." Grammatically, *mustaqīman* ("straight") is placed not as an adjective of the path but as an adverbial state — a placement implying that a path proposed by the Lord of the universe admits no possibility other than being straight (so Rūḥ al-Maʿānī and al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ).

"We have detailed Our Ayat" — *faṣṣalnā*, from *tafṣīl*, to describe a subject by analysing it unit by unit until no brevity or ambiguity remains. Yet the ayah restricts the benefit: "for a people who take heed." The Qur'an is clear, but only those approach it profitably who come without doggedness, opinionatedness, or the barriers of blind adherence to ancestral ways — exactly the plea of the luxuried deniers in the ayah Ibn Kathir quoted at 123: "We found our fathers following a certain way and religion, and we will indeed follow their footsteps" (43:23).

## The Abode of Peace (ayah 127)

The passage that opened with a man given light to walk through this world ends with where the walking leads: "For them will be the abode of peace with their Lord. And He will be their Wali because of what they used to do."

*Dār as-Salām*: *dār* is an abode; *salām* is peace and security from every calamity, catastrophe and hardship — so this is a home which sorrow and pain can never enter, and that can only be Paradise. Ibn ʿAbbas gave a second reading: *as-Salām* is a name of Allah, so this is the abode of Allah — and the abode of Allah is, of necessity, a place of peace. Ibn Kathir notes why Paradise bears this name here: its residents are safe because of their access to the straight path just mentioned, which conforms to the way of the Prophets; and just as their way was not wicked, they earned the abode of peace, free from all wickedness.

"With their Lord," says Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān, carries two assurances at once: they will receive it when they go to their Lord on the Day of Qiyamah, and the promise itself lies safe with Him — the most gracious Rabb is its guarantor, and no one can imagine, within the limits of this world, what He is keeping. Maʿārif even suggests that some servants are given a *taste* of the Abode of Peace here: hearts so attuned to the coming reward that "even stockpiles of suffering are reduced to a blade of grass" — just as a worker cheerfully bears a month's labour for the salary he can already see coming.

And the final word: "He will be their Wali" — their Protector, Supporter and Helper — "because of what they used to do." Deeds done in the light of ayah 122 end in the guardianship of Allah Himself, where everything hard becomes easy. The one left in the darknesses could never come out; the one given light walks all the way home.

passages.title: Jinn and humans judged after messengers were sent
passages.tafsir:
This passage is a single courtroom scene from the Day of Resurrection, together with the principles of justice that stand behind its verdict. Allah gathers the jinn and mankind and puts two questions. The first is addressed to the jinn who misled — and the Qur'an records no reply from them; it is their human allies who speak, confessing the "benefit" each side took from the other. The second question is put to jinn and mankind together — did messengers not come to you? — and this time they can only bear witness against themselves. Around these two exchanges, Allah unveils the laws behind the judgment: wrongdoers are made supporters of one another (ayah 129), no people is ever punished before being warned (ayah 131), and every soul receives a rank measured exactly by its deeds (ayah 132). What holds the five ayat together is one idea: on that Day, no one will have an excuse.

## The scene: misleaders and their allies before their Lord

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah commands His Prophet ﷺ — "Mention, O Muhammad, in what you convey and warn" — the Day when He gathers the jinn together with their loyal supporters from mankind: those who used to worship them in this life, seek refuge with them, obey them, and "inspire each other with adorned, deceitful speech." Then comes the proclamation: *"O you assembly of Jinn! Many did you mislead of men"* — that is, you misguided them and led them astray. Ibn Kathir connects this to Sūrah Yā Sīn (36:60–62), where Allah reminds the children of Adam of His command that they should not worship Shayṭān, a plain enemy to them — "And indeed he (Shaytan) did lead astray a great multitude of you."

Notice what the Qur'an does not record: any reply from the jinn. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Rūḥ al-Maʿānī, sees a deliberate hint in this silence — before the All-Knowing and All-Aware there was not much they could do but confess, and they will be so confounded by the question that they will not know how to make an answer. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that although the opening question was addressed to the satans of the jinn, the "human satans" — those who followed the satans' instigations, went astray themselves, and kept becoming the cause of others going astray — were its implied addressees too, since they had done the same work; and that is why their reply is the one recorded.

So it is the jinn's human allies who speak: *"Our Lord! We benefited one from the other, but now we have reached our appointed term which You did appoint for us."* The early scholar al-Ḥasan explained the mutual benefit starkly: "They benefited from each other when the Jinns merely commanded and mankind obeyed." Ibn Jurayj recalled the practice of the Jāhiliyyah (the pre-Islamic age of ignorance): a man would reach a land and proclaim, "I seek refuge with the master (Jinn) of this valley" — this, he said, is how they benefited from each other, and they used it as an excuse on the Day of Resurrection. The jinn's gain, Ibn Kathir notes, was that humans revered them by invoking them for help — so that they would proclaim, "We became the masters of both mankind and the Jinns." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the exchange further: the human satans learned from the jinn the ways of securing gratification from worldly enjoyments and at times called on them for help, while the satans among the jinn found a pliable people who listened to them and followed their dictates, so much so that they forgot all about death and the Hereafter. The "appointed term" the humans now admit to having reached is, according to as-Suddī, death — and what they had forgotten they now see in front of them.

Then the verdict: *"The Fire be your dwelling place, you will dwell therein forever, except as Allah may will."* What of that exception clause? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers directly: the definitive statements of the Qur'an (nuṣūṣ) establish that Allah would not so will for them — so their stay is truly forever. And the ayah seals the sentence with His names: *"Certainly your Lord is All-Wise, All-Knowing."*

The scene resumes in ayah 130, and now the question is put to both species at once: *"Did not there come to you Messengers from amongst you, reciting unto you My verses and warning you of the meeting of this Day of yours?"* Ibn Kathir observes that Allah asks them "while having better knowledge." They will say: *"We bear witness against ourselves"* — meaning, Ibn Kathir explains, we affirm that the Messengers conveyed Your messages to us and warned us of the meeting with You, and that this Day would certainly occur. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that they were being asked to show the reason why they chose to disbelieve and disobey — and no reason for their wrongdoing was given from their side. Allah Himself supplies it: *"It was the life of this world that deceived them."* The charms of a transitory life put them on the wrong track: "They thought that it was everything, which was really nothing," and it left them heedless of their end.

A confession — but do not other ayat say they will deny? Elsewhere the Qur'an reports the disbelievers swearing, "we swear by Allah, our Lord, we were no mushriks" — a mushrik being one who ascribes partners to Allah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān resolves the apparent contradiction through further verses: they will first deny; then Allah, in His perfect power, will make them speechless, and witnesses will come from the different parts of their own bodies; then Allah will give them their speech back, and they will tell everything about their misdeeds openly and clearly. Left with no room to deny, they confess. Denial, exposure, confession: each ayah describes one stage.

## "Thus We do make the wrongdoers supporters of one another"

Between the two exchanges of the courtroom stands ayah 129, which states the law the whole scene illustrates. Much turns on one Arabic word, nuwallī. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that lexically it can be translated either in the sense of joining up and bringing closer, or in the sense of setting on and imposing on — and narrations from the leading authorities in tafsir among the Ṣaḥābah (the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ) and the Tābiʿīn (the generation who learned from them) explain the word in both of these senses.

**First sense — like is joined with like.** The early authorities Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Qatādah and others read the ayah as describing the groupings of the Resurrection: on the day of Qiyāmah (the Resurrection), people will not be formed into groups on a racial, national, colour or language basis, but on the basis of deeds and morals. A Muslim obedient to Allah, wherever he may be, shall be together with the Muslims; the disobedient disbeliever, wherever he may be, shall be together with the disbelievers — and even among Muslims, those good in deeds shall be with the righteous while the evildoers are grouped with evildoers and sinners. This is the sense of the verse of Sūrah at-Takwīr, "when people shall be grouped (like with like)." ʿUmar al-Fārūq, may Allah be pleased with him, explained the ayah exactly this way: "The doers of one kind of deeds, good or bad, shall be grouped together. The good will go with the good to Jannah and the evil will be led with the evil to Jahannam" — Jannah being Paradise and Jahannam the Fire — and he cited as proof 37:22: "Gather those who have been unjust, and their cohorts, (and take them to Jahannam)." Qatādah, as Ibn Kathir reports, put it grimly: "Allah makes the wrongdoers supporters for each other in the Fire by following one another into it."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out how this law already operates in this world. A good person is temperamentally tuned to virtues and virtuous people; his attachment to them becomes his passport to ever-new avenues of good deeds, which in turn make his determination firm. The evildoer likewise relates to his own kind, and that negative company keeps contributing to his evil deeds and evil morals, until "avenues of good and prospects of better conduct keep closing on him before his own eyes" — his "cash punishment," received right here in this world before the Hereafter ever arrives. The Prophet ﷺ is reported to have said that when Allah is pleased with a ruler, He gives him good ministers and good staff who make his government well-managed; and when Allah is displeased with someone, he gets colleagues and officials who are bad, so that even if he wishes to do something good, he cannot get it done.

**Second sense — one oppressor is set upon another.** Reported from ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAbbās, ʿAbdullah ibn az-Zubayr, Ibn Zayd, Mālik ibn Dīnār and others, may Allah be pleased with them: Allah sets some unjust people over other unjust people, and thus has one ẓālim (oppressor) punished at the hands of another ẓālim. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān affirms that "this approach to meaning is also correct and sound in its place, and is in accord with other statements of the Qur'an and Hadith." ʿAbdur-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam linked it to 43:36 — "And whosoever turns away blindly from the remembrance of the Most Gracious (Allah), We appoint for him Shaytan to be a companion to him" — and said: "We appoint the wrongdoer of the Jinns over the wrongdoer of mankind." Ibn Kathir quotes a poet's line: "There is no hand, but Allah's Hand is above it, and no wrongdoer but will be tested by another wrongdoer." And he sums up the ayah: "Just as We made this losing group of mankind supporters of the Jinns that misguided them, We also appoint the wrongdoers over one another, destroy them by the hands of one another, and take revenge from them with one another. This is the just recompense for their injustice and transgression."

The Prophet ﷺ is reported to have said: "as you shall be, so shall be the rulers set on you" — if you are unjust and evil, your rulers will also be unjust and evil; and if you are good in your deeds and characters, Allah will make good, kind and just people your rulers. Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him, said the same: when Allah wishes well for a people, He appoints the best rulers and officials for them, and when He wishes otherwise for a people, He sets the worst rulers and officials over them (Tafsir al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ). According to Rūḥ al-Maʿānī, it is on the authority of this very ayah that Muslim jurists prove that when the people of a country turn away from Allah and become involved in deeds of injustice and oppression, Allah sets oppressive rulers and officials over them and lets them be punished at their hands. And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that Ibn Kathir has reported, based on a narration by ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿūd, may Allah be pleased with him, a decisive statement of the Prophet ﷺ: whoever helps a ẓālim in his ẓulm (injustice), Allah sets that very ẓālim on him to torment him, and it is at his hands that he gets his punishment.

## Were there messengers among the jinn?

The courtroom question of ayah 130 — *"Did not there come to you Messengers from amongst you?"* — is addressed to jinn and mankind together, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that on its face this shows messengers were sent to the jinn-kind from among their own kind, just as human messengers were sent to human beings. On this question, the scholars of tafsir and hadith genuinely differed.

One position, which Ibn Kathir argues at length and attributes to Mujāhid, Ibn Jurayj and others among the Imams of the Salaf (the early generations) and later scholars, is that messengers have only ever been from mankind. He marshals the proofs: Allah sent revelation to Nūḥ, peace be upon him, and the prophets after him — "Messengers as bearers of good news as well as of warning in order that mankind should have no plea against Allah after the (coming of) Messengers" (4:163–165); He ordained prophethood and the Book exclusively in the offspring of Ibrāhīm (29:27) — and, in Ibn Kathir's own words, "No one has claimed that there were Prophets from among the Jinns before the time of Ibrahim, but not after that"; and of all the messengers Allah says, "verily, they ate food and walked in the markets" (25:20), and "We sent not before you any but men unto whom We revealed, from among the people of townships" (12:109). Therefore, Ibn Kathir concludes, "concerning prophethood, the Jinns follow mankind." What the jinn had were warners of their own kind: in 46:29–32 a group of jinn listen to the Qur'an and return "to their people, as warners," calling them to respond to Allah's caller; and in Sūrah al-Jinn they say, "Indeed, we have heard a wonderful Qur'an that leads to rectitude, so in it we believe" (72:1). It is in this context that Ibn Kathir cites a hadith collected by At-Tirmidhi: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited Sūrat Ar-Raḥmān to these jinn — the sūrah in which Allah addresses "you two classes (Jinn and men)" together (55:31–32). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains how this position satisfies the ayah's wording: such believing jinn were really couriers and message-bearers of a messenger, and so they too can be called rusul within the literal sense of that Arabic word — a rasūl is, literally, a carrier of a message.

A second group of scholars, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records, took the outward meaning of the verse: before the appearance of the Last of the Prophets ﷺ, each of the two species had messengers from among its own kind — human messengers to human beings, and messengers to the classes of the jinn from their kind only. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān goes on to state the distinction of the Last of the Prophets ﷺ: he was sent as the only messenger for all human beings and all the jinn of the whole world, and not for one given time only — all human beings and jinn born right up to the Last Day shall be his community, and he alone shall be their messenger and prophet.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a related note from Tafsir Mazhari: following Kalbī and Mujāhid, Qāḍī Thanāʼullah of Panipat reasoned that since the jinn inhabited the earth thousands of years before human beings and are likewise obligated by the Shari'ah, they too must have had prophets among them — and he suggests, as a probability and not a certainty, that the "Autars" (avatars) of the Hindus may have been these very messengers of the jinn-kind or their deputies, their book later altered into idolatry and shirk (the ascribing of partners to Allah); and in any case it would stand abrogated after the appearance of the Prophet ﷺ and the universal application of his prophethood.

## Warned before punished, ranked exactly by deeds

*"This is because your Lord would not destroy the (populations of) towns for their wrongdoing while their people were unaware."* Ayah 131 gives the reason for the whole apparatus of prophethood the courtroom has just invoked. Ibn Kathir paraphrases: We sent the Messengers and revealed the Books to the jinn and mankind so that no one has an excuse that he is being punished for his wrongs although he did not receive Allah's message; We did not punish any of the nations except after sending Messengers to them. He stacks up the parallel ayat: "And there never was a nation but a warner had passed among them" (35:24); "And verily, We have sent among every Ummah a Messenger" (16:36); "And We never punish until We have sent a Messenger" (17:15); and the exchange at the gate of Hell — "Did no warner come to you?" "Yes, indeed a warner did come to us, but we belied him" (67:8–9). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān distils it into one sentence: sending prophets and messengers among human beings and the jinn is based on the dictate of the justice and mercy of Allah, for He does not send punishment over a people unless they have been awakened through His blessed messengers and provided with the light of guidance.

Then, in ayah 132, the measure of the verdicts: *"For all there will be degrees according to what they did."* At-Ṭabarī read it broadly: "every person who obeys Allah or behaves disobediently, has grades and ranks according to their works, which Allah gives them as recompense, good for good and evil for evil." Ibn Kathir adds that it is possible the ayah refers specifically to the disbelievers of the jinn and mankind, who will earn a place in the Fire according to their evil deeds — citing "For each one there is double (torment)" (7:38) and "Those who disbelieved and hinder (others) from the path of Allah, for them We will add torment to the torment because they used to spread corruption" (16:88). On either reading, the measure is deeds. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states it plainly: with Allah there are ranks for the classes of people among human beings and the jinn, assigned in terms of their deeds — and when they are rewarded or punished, the measure used shall be that of their deeds.

And the guarantee that the calibration is exact: *"And your Lord is not unaware of what they do."* Ibn Jarir comments that all these deeds that they did, they did while your Lord was aware of them; He collects and records them with Him, so that He recompenses them when they meet Him and return to Him.

## Living it

The passage's practical weight sits in ayah 129. If Allah's law is that people are allied — in this world and in the Hereafter — with those who resemble them in deed, then your company is not a neutral fact about you; it shapes what you become. The sources draw three concrete lines. Choose companions whose goodness opens avenues of good for you, for evil company closes those avenues, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, "before his own eyes." Remember the reported words of the Prophet ﷺ — "as you shall be, so shall be the rulers set on you" — for if a people are good in their deeds and characters, Allah makes good, kind and just people their rulers. And never lend a hand to an oppressor, for the reported warning of the Prophet ﷺ is that Allah will set that very oppressor upon his helper, and at his hands he will receive his punishment. Behind it all stands ayah 131's immense comfort: the Lord who will judge with such exactness is a Lord who never punished any nation He had not first warned.

passages.title: The Self-Sufficient Lord's promise will come
passages.tafsir:
# The Self-Sufficient Lord's Promise Will Come (6:133–135)

These three ayat close a long discussion about why Allah sends messengers and warns nations before ever punishing them. They answer the question that discussion leaves hanging: *why does Allah bother?* The answer given in ayah 133 is breathtaking — not because He needs anything from us, for He is utterly free of need, but out of pure mercy. And because He needs nothing from us, His promise stands regardless of whether anyone accepts it (ayah 134), and His Prophet ﷺ can issue the calm, confident challenge of ayah 135: carry on your way; I will carry on mine; we shall soon see whose end is the happy one. What holds the passage together is a single movement of thought — from *who Allah is*, to *what must therefore come*, to *how a believer stands* while waiting for it.

## Two names deliberately paired: al-Ghani, Dhū al-Raḥmah

Ayah 133 opens: **"Your Lord is al-Ghani, Dhū al-Raḥmah"** — the Self-Sufficient, the Master of Mercy. Ibn Kathir explains *al-Ghani* as the One who is Rich, free from needing His creatures in any way or form, **while they stand in need of Him in all situations** — and *Dhū al-Raḥmah* as full of mercy towards creation, citing the parallel ayah, "Truly, Allah is full of kindness, the Most Merciful towards mankind" (2:143).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out why *these two names in this order* unlock the whole passage. The preceding verses established that Allah always sent messengers to warn people before punishing them. Someone might imagine this means Allah somehow *needed* our obedience and worship, or that some task of His depended on it. The verse cuts that thought off at the root: He is absolutely All-Independent. But alongside that perfect freedom from need stands the attribute of mercy — and **mercy, not need, is the real cause of sending messengers and books** for the good of human beings.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also notices a fine point of wording. The Qur'an could have used a single name here — *ar-Raḥmān* (All-Merciful) or *ar-Raḥīm* (Very-Merciful) — and the meaning "Allah is merciful" would have been conveyed. Instead it chose the compound form *Dhū al-Raḥmah*, "The Master of Mercy," precisely because sitting next to *al-Ghani* it displays the **correlation** between the two attributes: He who depends on no one, and on nothing in the universe, is at the same time the one who has mercy and dispenses it at will.

The commentary presses the point with an observation anyone can verify: the greatest blessings we have were never asked for. No human being ever prayed to be born — praying before existing cannot even be imagined. No one requested eyes, ears, hands, feet, a heart, a brain. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, we were not there, we did not ask — **it was His mercy hearing the unsaid**.

**A subtle wisdom about human need.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a striking reflection: Allah, who is Himself need-free, deliberately made no human being need-free. When people feel themselves free of needs, they stop caring for others and turn readily to injustice — the commentary cites the Qur'an itself (96:6): when human beings find themselves need-free and independent, they are ready to rebel and transgress. So Allah tied human beings together in mutual dependence: the king needs his retinue, the wealthy man needs help, the industrialist depends on his labour; the driver comes out to earn his day's living while the one who can pay must hail him. No one is doing anyone a favour — nature has chained them together. All of this, the commentary says, is a manifestation of the most perfect attribute of the One who is All-Independent, yet the Master of Mercy.

## "If He wills, He can take you away"

The second half of ayah 133 turns the same truth into a warning: *if He wills, He can take you away and bring in your place whomever He wills, just as He raised you from the seed of other people.* Ibn Kathir explains: if you defy His commandments He can remove you and replace you with successors who behave obediently — and this is easy for Him, just as He destroyed earlier nations and raised their successors. Ibn Kathir gathers the sister-verses that make the same point: "If He wills, He can take you away, O people, and bring others" (4:133); "O mankind! It is you who stand in need of Allah… If He willed, He could destroy you and bring about a new creation, and that is not hard for Allah" (35:15–17); "Allah is Rich and you are poor. And if you turn away, He will exchange you for some other people, and they will not be your likes" (47:38).

On the phrase "from the seed (*dhurriyyah*) of other people," Ibn Kathir records the explanation of Aban bin 'Uthman (transmitted through Muhammad bin Ishaq from Ya'qub bin 'Utbah): "the seed means the offspring and the children" — you yourselves are simply the descendants of a generation that has already gone.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lingers on the verb **yudhhibkum**, "He shall take you away." Notice what the verse does *not* say: it does not speak of destroying, killing or exterminating. "Taking away" denotes something quieter and more total — unmaking, un-being, the loss of name, identity and trace. And the proof of how effortlessly this happens lies before every generation. Think of the millions who inhabit the earth today and run its affairs; then think back a hundred years. The earth was just as inhabited, business went on as usual — yet not one of today's movers and shakers was there. That entire population now lies beneath the earth with no trace to be found, and we are merely their descendants. Allah has, in fact, been quietly "taking away" and replacing humanity all along.

## Ayah 134: a promise that cannot be dodged

**"Indeed, what you have been promised will certainly come to pass, and you cannot escape."** The two commentaries bring out two dimensions of "what you are promised," and they complete each other. Ibn Kathir reads it of the **Resurrection**: tell them, O Muhammad ﷺ, that what they have been promised of Resurrection will surely occur, and they cannot escape from Allah — rather, He is able to resurrect them even after they have become dust and bones, for Allah is able to do all things and nothing ever escapes His power. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads it of the **divine punishment** promised to the disobedient: it is bound to come, and you cannot frustrate it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān itself ties this warning back to ayah 133: having established in the first verse that Allah is All-Independent, Master of Mercy — and All-Powerful too — the text now carries its warning to the disobedient. On either reading the door is shut: you cannot escape from Allah, and you cannot frustrate what He has promised.

## Ayah 135: "Carry on your way — and you will come to know"

The passage ends with Allah instructing His Prophet ﷺ what to say to his people in Makkah: **"O my people! Work according to your way, surely, I too am working, and you will come to know for whom is the ultimate abode. Certainly the wrongdoers will not be successful."**

The key word is *makānatikum*. Ibn Kathir records from Ibn 'Abbas (through 'Ali bin Abi Talhah) that it means **"your way."** So the sense is: remain on your path if you insist you are rightly guided, and I will remain on mine. Ibn Kathir calls this "a stern warning and a sure promise" in one breath, pointing to its twin in 11:121–122: "Act according to your way, we are acting… And you wait! We too are waiting." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that this was another method of awakening the heedless: the choice not to accept is theirs; let them keep doing what their belief and hostility dictate, and the Prophet ﷺ will keep doing what his belief dictates — in that there is no loss for him — but very soon they will be the ones to find out who is blessed with the ultimate salvation and success. This is not a shrug of indifference; it is the composure of someone certain of the verdict.

**A precision in the wording that Ibn Kathir caught.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān highlights Ibn Kathir's observation about the exact words of the text: *ʿāqibat ad-dār* — "the ultimate abode." The verse does *not* say *ʿāqibat ad-dār al-ākhirah*, "the ultimate abode **of the Hereafter**." The omission is meaningful: much earlier than the abode of the Hereafter, the ultimate success falls to the righteous servants of Allah **even within the present abode of the world**.

And history sealed the point. Ibn Kathir writes that Allah indeed kept His promise: He allowed Muhammad ﷺ to prevail in the land over those who defied him, conquered Makkah for him, and made him triumphant over the very people who had rejected him and shown him enmity. Within his own lifetime his rule spread over the Arabian Peninsula, Yemen and Bahrain; after his passing, land after land was opened during the time of his successors, may Allah be pleased with them all. Ibn Kathir then sets this history beside Allah's own decrees: "Allah has decreed: Verily, it is I and My Messengers who shall be the victorious. Verily, Allah is All-Powerful, Almighty" (58:21); "Verily, We will indeed make victorious Our Messengers and those who believe in this world's life and on the Day when the witnesses will stand forth. The Day when their excuses will be of no profit to the wrongdoers. Theirs will be the curse, and theirs will be the evil abode" (40:51–52); "And indeed We have written in the Zabur, after the Dhikr, that My righteous servants shall inherit the land" (21:105). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reaches the same verdict — within the period of prophethood the whole of Arabia came under the Prophet's ﷺ authority, soon extending to Yemen, Bahrain and the borders of Syria, and at the hands of his successors and Companions a major part of the known world of the time came under their aegis — declaring the promise of Allah fulfilled and citing the decree of 58:21 and the promise of help in 40:51.

The passage closes on its unbending moral law: **"Certainly the ẓālimūn will not be successful"** — the wrongdoers, those Maʿārif ul Qurʼān glosses as the unjust, the usurpers of rights. Whatever they seem to win in the short term, real success — in this abode or the next — is simply never theirs.

## Living it

Two things follow directly from this passage. First, worship and obedience add nothing to Allah and their absence takes nothing from Him — He is al-Ghani, free from needing His creatures in any way, while we stand in need of Him in all situations. Every messenger and every book He sent was therefore sent out of mercy, for our good. Second, the believer's posture before a mocking, hostile world is the one taught to the Prophet ﷺ in ayah 135 — no panic, no compulsion, no need to force the verdict early. Keep working on your way, with the settled certainty that the promise of the Self-Sufficient Lord is already on its way and no one can hold it back.

passages.title: Pagan superstitions over crops, cattle, and children
passages.tafsir:
This passage is a portrait of religion invented by human beings: the pagans of Arabia carving up Allah's own gifts — crops, cattle, even their children — according to superstitions their idols and devils dictated to them. What holds ayat 136–140 together is a single charge repeated in different forms: *they legislated in Allah's name without Allah's permission*, and every one of their man-made rules ended up cheating Allah, harming themselves, and wronging the weak. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the linkage: the previous verses exposed the **false beliefs** of the mushriks (those who associate partners with Allah), and these verses now expose their **practical errors and ignorant customs** — belief gone wrong always becomes life gone wrong.

## The rigged division (ayah 136)

The first custom sounds almost pious. At harvest time the pagans would divide their produce and livestock: "This is for Allah, and this is for our partners" — their idols. The portion for Allah went to the poor and needy; the portion for the idols went to the priests and keepers of the idol-temples, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains.

But watch what happened in practice. Ibn Kathir relays the account that ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah and al-ʿAwfī narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās: whenever they cultivated land or gathered produce, they assigned one part to Allah and another to the idol — and then guarded the idol's share with obsessive care. Anything that accidentally fell from the share assigned to Allah, they collected and added to the idol's share. If water assigned to the idol irrigated something assigned to Allah, whatever that water irrigated was added to the idol's share. If land or produce assigned to Allah was accidentally mixed with the idol's share, they said "the idol is poor," left it with the idol, and would not return it to Allah's portion. And if water assigned to Allah irrigated what was assigned to the idol, the produce was — once again — left for the idol. In the same narration Ibn ʿAbbās adds that they consecrated other property besides, the **Baḥīrah, Sāʾibah, Waṣīlah and Ḥām**, assigning them to the idols while claiming they did so as a means of approach to Allah. Similar explanations, Ibn Kathir notes, came from Mujāhid, Qatādah and as-Suddī.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the same crookedness from another angle. If there was a drop in the produce, the whole shortfall was applied against Allah's portion, "for Allah is Independent and does not need it" — while the idols' portion, and their own, were exacted in full. If something from the idols' portion, or from their own, happened to fall into the portion reserved for Allah, they would pick it up and take it out again to keep their accounting straight; but if anything of Allah's portion fell in with theirs or the idols', it was left where it lay, with the same excuse: Allah is need-free, so a cut in His share does no harm — but the "partners" need theirs in full.

This is what the ayah means by "the share of their partners reaches not Allah, while the share of Allah reaches their partners." Every accounting question was resolved in the idol's favour. ʿAbdur-Raḥmān bin Zayd bin Aslam adds another layer: even the animals they "dedicated to Allah" would not be eaten unless the idols' names were pronounced at slaughter — while animals sacrificed to the idols never had Allah's Name mentioned over them at all. The dedication to Allah was a label; the substance always flowed to the idols.

Hence the verdict that closes the ayah: **sāʾa mā yaḥkumūn** — "Evil is the way they judge!" Ibn Kathir draws out the real absurdity: Allah is the Lord, Owner and Creator of *all* things — the ayah pointedly says the crops and cattle are "of that which **He** created." To assign the Creator a "share" of His own creation was error enough; and even that evil division they did not preserve, but cheated in it. Ibn Kathir links it to the same lopsided arithmetic elsewhere in the Qur'an: they assigned daughters to Allah while keeping for themselves what they desired (16:57); they assigned to some of His own servants "a share with Him" — "Verily, man is indeed a manifest ingrate!" (43:15); "Is it for you the males and for Him the females? That indeed is a division most unfair!" (53:21–22).

## Devils who made child-killing look good (ayah 137)

Ayah 137 begins "and likewise" (*wa-kadhālika*): the same "partners" who dictated the crooked harvest-division "made fair-seeming to many of the idolators the killing of their children." Ibn Kathir explains the mechanism: just as the shayāṭīn (devils) lured them into the share-splitting, they beautified infanticide — killing children for fear of poverty, and burying daughters alive for fear of dishonour. Ibn ʿAbbās, in the report of ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah, put it simply: "They make killing their children attractive to them." Mujāhid says the "partners" here are the devils, who *ordered* them to bury their children for fear of poverty; as-Suddī says the devils commanded the killing of daughters with two aims, both named in the ayah: **li-yurdūhum** — "to lead them to their own destruction" — and **li-yalbisū ʿalayhim dīnahum** — "to cause confusion in their religion." Notice the word "fair-seeming" (*zayyana*): the horror of this custom was not sold as horror. It was dressed up as prudence, honour, even piety. That is how Shayṭān works — he does not advertise destruction; he decorates it.

Then comes a sentence that matters for creed: "And if Allah had willed, they would not have done so." Ibn Kathir explains: all of this occurred by Allah's leave, will and decree — yet **He dislikes these practices** — and He has perfect wisdom in every decree. "He is never questioned about what He does, but they all will be questioned." And so the Prophet ﷺ is told: "leave them alone with their fabrications" — avoid and abandon them and what they invent, for Allah will judge between you and them.

## Taboos invented in Allah's name (ayah 138)

Ayah 138 turns to their food-law inventions. They declared certain cattle and crops **ḥijr** — Ibn ʿAbbās explains the word as "what they forbade," made off-limits, "such as the Waṣīlah and the like" — and said "none may eat of them except those whom we allow." As-Suddī spells out the claim: only those whom *we* choose may eat of them; everyone else is barred. Qatādah's comment cuts to the bone: this was "a prohibition that the shayāṭīn appointed for their wealth, and a type of exaggeration and extremism **that did not come from Allah**." That is the whole indictment in one line: religion has one Legislator, and these laws had a different author.

The bundle's sources sketch the system in detail. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (drawing on narrations from Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Ibn Zayd and as-Suddī, as gathered in ad-Durr al-Manthūr and Rūḥ al-Maʿānī) lists the customs of Jāhiliyyah — the pre-Islamic "age of ignorance" — that these verses answer. Four classes of animal, the **Baḥīrah, Sāʾibah, Waṣīlah and Ḥām**, were released or consecrated in the name of the idols, and revering them was itself treated as an act of worship. These animals could not be ridden or loaded; Abū Wāʾil explained that the Baḥīrah would not even be used for Ḥajj, whether by riding it or carrying things on it. Mujāhid mentions camels belonging to the idolators over which Allah's Name was never pronounced — not when riding, milking, carrying things, mating, or in any other action; as-Suddī adds that the cattle forbidden for burden were the Baḥīrah, Sāʾibah, Waṣīlah and Ḥām, together with cattle over which the idolators would not mention Allah's Name when slaughtering them, nor when they were born. Ibn Kathir cites the parallel verse: "Allah has not instituted a Baḥīrah or a Sāʾibah or a Waṣīlah or a Ḥām — but those who disbelieve invent lies against Allah" (5:103), and the challenge of 10:59: "Tell me, what provision Allah has sent down to you! And you have made of it lawful and unlawful. Say: Has Allah permitted you, or do you invent a lie against Allah?"

The ayah stamps the whole system with its true name: **iftirāʾan ʿalayh** — "lying against Him." Ibn Kathir: the idolators indeed lied when they attributed this evil to Allah's religion and Law, for He did not allow them to do that, nor did He approve of it — "He will recompense them for what they used to fabricate" against Him and falsely attribute to Him.

## A religion rigged against women (ayah 139)

Ayah 139 exposes the ugliest feature of this system: it was rigged against women. "What is in the bellies of such and such cattle is exclusively for our males and forbidden to our females — but if it is born dead, then they all share in it." Ibn ʿAbbās explains that this refers to the **milk** of the consecrated animals, which they prohibited for their females and allowed only their males to drink, and to the **offspring**: when a sheep gave birth to a male, they would slaughter it and feed it to their males, not their females; if the newborn was a female they would not slaughter it; but if it was stillborn, males and females would share in it. "Allah forbade this practice" — and as-Suddī said the same. Ash-Shaʿbī describes the same rule for the Baḥīrah: its milk was only given to the men, but if any of its cattle died, men and women alike shared in eating it — and similar was said by ʿIkrimah, Qatādah and ʿAbdur-Raḥmān bin Zayd bin Aslam. Mujāhid comments that the ayah refers to the Sāʾibah and the Baḥīrah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that they endowed tillage and cattle the same way — produce for men only, women given a share purely at men's whim, with no right to demand.

Look at the shape of this "religion": the choice cuts went to men, the carrion was generously shared with women, and the whole thing was stamped with divine authority. The ayah closes with the sentence: **sayajzīhim waṣfahum** — "He will punish them for their attribution." Abū al-ʿĀliyah, Mujāhid and Qatādah explain: for uttering such falsehood. Ibn Kathir points to 16:116 as the standing warning: "Say not, concerning that which your tongues falsely utter, 'This is lawful and this is forbidden,' so as to invent lies against Allah — verily, those who invent lies against Allah will never prosper." And the ayah ends: "Verily, He is All-Wise, All-Knower" — Wise in His actions, statements, Law and decree; Knowing of the actions of His servants, good or evil, and He will recompense them for these deeds completely.

## The verdict: lost twice over (ayah 140)

Ayah 140 pronounces sentence: "Lost indeed are those who killed their children foolishly, without knowledge, and forbade what Allah provided for them, inventing a lie against Allah. They have gone astray and were never guided."

Ibn Kathir spells out the double loss. **In this world**: they killed their own children — destroying their families with their own hands — and made life difficult for themselves by prohibiting some types of their wealth, "as an act of innovation that they invented on their own." Superstition is expensive: it cost them their sons and daughters and their sustenance. **In the Hereafter**: they will end up in the worst of dwellings, because they used to lie about Allah and invent falsehood about Him, as in 10:69–70 — "those who invent a lie against Allah will never be successful; a brief enjoyment in this world, then unto Us is their return, then We shall make them taste the severest torment."

Ibn Kathir then records a striking remark of Ibn ʿAbbās, related by al-Ḥāfiẓ Abū Bakr bin Marduwyah and also recorded by al-Bukhārī in the section of his Ṣaḥīḥ on the virtues of the Quraysh: "If it pleases you to know how ignorant the Arabs used to be, then recite the ayat beyond ayah one hundred and thirty in Sūrat al-Anʿām" — and he recited this very verse. In other words: if you want a definition of Jāhiliyyah, here it is — people who murdered their children out of "wisdom" and starved themselves out of "piety."

## Reading these ayat today

Two threads from the sources are worth carrying home.

**First, the principle beneath the stories.** Every custom in this passage — the rigged shares, the sacred camels, the men-only milk — fails the same single test Qatādah applied: *it did not come from Allah*. The right to declare things lawful and forbidden, and the right to a share of what He created, belong to Allah alone. Any religiosity that Allah did not legislate, however solemn it looks, is ḥijr all over again — "exaggeration and extremism that did not come from Allah."

**Second, the mirror Maʿārif ul Qurʼān holds up to Muslims.** The pagans' accounting trick — every shortfall deducted from Allah's share, because "Allah is need-free" — has a modern echo. Our life, our body and mind, are given by Allah, and His right demanded that all our living years be devoted to obeying and worshipping Him. Yet when we do set aside a portion of our day for prayer, remembrance and reciting the Qur'an, watch what happens the moment an urgent need arrives — a call, an appointment, a business matter, sickness: the work stays, the rest-time stays, and the axe falls precisely on the time we had ear-marked for our dhikr and ʿibādah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names this for what it is — wrong, ungrateful, and a compromising of Allah's right — and closes with the prayer worth repeating: may Allah Taʿālā keep us and all Muslims protected from it.

passages.title: Allah's produce and cattle refute invented taboos
passages.tafsir:
This passage closes Sūrah al-Anʿām's long exposure of the invented religion of the Makkan pagans by calling the evidence itself to the stand: the gardens, crops and cattle over which they had legislated their taboos. Ayah 141 walks through the orchard and closes with its own commands — eat of its fruit when it bears fruit, pay its due on the day of its harvest, and waste not. Ayah 142 walks through the herd and adds the decisive one: eat of what Allah has provided, and follow not the footsteps of Shaytan. Then ayat 143–144 put the pagans under cross-examination, species by species, until their whole system of forbidden camels and men-only milk collapses under one question: were you there when Allah ordered this?

## The religion being refuted

Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān explains the linkage: the previous verses recounted the false *beliefs* of the mushriks of Arabia; these verses turn to their *practical* errors — ignorance-based customs to which they had given legal status. The list it draws from Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Ibn Zayd and as-Suddī is startling in its detail. They divided grain and fruit into a portion "for Allah" and a portion for the idols — and whenever the shares got mixed, the accounting always favoured the idols, on the excuse that Allah is need-free and the "partners" are not. They released animals in the name of idols, calling them Baḥīrah and Sāʾibah, and claimed they were doing it for Allah's pleasure. Produce of certain fields, meat of certain animals, even milk, was declared lawful for men and unlawful for women — and if a calf was born dead, suddenly everyone could eat it. They revered four classes of designated animals — Baḥīrah, Sāʾibah, Waṣīlah and Ḥām — as an act of worship; these names, Ibn Kathir explains, were labels the pagans gave to cattle whose use they had prohibited, innovations they themselves invented for their cattle, fruits and produce. And they killed their female children. Ibn Kathir summarises the whole disease in one line: the idolators "mishandled by their misguided ideas" the very produce and cattle Allah had created, "dividing them into various designated parts, allowing some and prohibiting some."

Against this backdrop the passage's opening words carry their full weight: **"He is the One Who produces…"** Everything you are rationing by superstition, He made.

## Ayah 141 — the orchard as witness

The verse names the garden world with precision, and the vocabulary matters. *Maʿrūshāt* comes from a root meaning to raise something high: these are the trellised plants, vines mounted on supports, like the grape. *Ghayr maʿrūshāt* — untrellised — covers everything else: trees standing on their own trunks, and creepers like the melon that spread along the ground. Ibn ʿAbbās explained it both ways in different reports preserved by Ibn Kathir: what people trellise versus what "grows wild inland and on mountains," or trellised versus untrellised grapevines. Then date-palms, crops of every kind, olives and pomegranates, "similar and not similar" — Ibn Jurayj said: similar in shape, but different in taste.

Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān lingers here, and it is worth lingering with it. The same soil, the same water, the same air and atmosphere — yet the grape is so made that it must climb or its fruit will not survive, while the melon is so made that its vine refuses to climb, and if it did, the fruit would weaken and wither. Some fruits ripen lying on the earth; a touch of soil would spoil others, which must hang from high branches in the air and the sun to take their colour. "This talisman of trees," Maʿārif says, "is not simply accidental. It has wisdom, intention and mastery of execution behind it" — and it seals the point with the Qur'an's own doxology, *"So blessed be Allah, the best of creators"* (23:14). This is a phenomenon that compels even a person of ordinary insight to recognise a Creator whose knowledge and wisdom cannot even be imagined. And that recognition is the argument of the whole passage: the One who alone designed all this is alone entitled to legislate about it. How, Maʿārif asks, could a people undermine their Powerful, Knowing Creator in favour of things weak, inert and unaware, and make *those* His partners in produce and worship?

## Eat — and give on the day of harvest

Two commands follow in ayah 141. First: **"Eat of its fruit when it bears fruit."** Maʿārif draws out the tenderness in this: the Creator did not make this array of fruits to fulfil any need of His own; it exists for your benefit — so eat and enjoy. And the phrase "when it bears fruit" carries a quiet reminder: making the fruit come out of the branch was never within your power; once it forms by Allah's permission, it is yours to eat, even before it fully ripens.

Second: **"and pay its due on the day of its harvest."** The *ḥaqq* — the "due" — is a right owed to the poor from the produce itself, and the early Muslims painted a vivid picture of it. Mujāhid said: when the poor are present on harvest day, give them some of the produce — and in another report, one gives away handfuls at planting, handfuls at harvest, and lets the poor glean whatever is left on the ground. Ibrāhīm an-Nakhaʿī said: one gives away some of the hay. And Saʿīd bin Jubayr, summing up the whole custom — the handfuls of seed grains given to the poor, and some of the hay as food for their animals — noted that this ruling "was before Zakah became obligatory."

That remark opens the classical question Maʿārif treats at length: is this "due" general charity, or the fixed Zakah of the land known as *ʿushr* (the "tenth")? Companions and Successors held both views, largely depending on whether they counted the verse as Makkan or Madinan, since Zakah's detailed obligation came two years after the Hijrah. Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-ʿArabī, as Maʿārif reports, resolved it elegantly: either way, the verse can mean the Zakah of the land — because the *principle* of Zakah had already been revealed in Makkah (in Sūrah al-Muzzammil), while its rates and thresholds were fixed only later. This verse establishes that a due is owed on the land's produce without quantifying it; in the unsettled Makkan years no quantity was needed, and generous people simply gave at harvest as charitable communities always had. After the Hijrah the Prophet ﷺ specified the amounts, in the narration Maʿārif says is reported in all Hadith books on the authority of Muʿādh ibn Jabal, Ibn ʿUmar and Jābir ibn ʿAbdullāh: one-tenth of the produce from land watered by rain, one-twentieth from land irrigated by wells.

Maʿārif uncovers the principle beneath these numbers: across the whole Law of Zakah, the less the labour and expense behind a gain, the higher its Zakah. Found treasure — one-fifth. Rain-fed land — one-tenth. Well-irrigated land — one-twentieth. Cash and trading goods, which cost the most effort — one-fortieth. And because neither this verse nor the hadith fixes any minimum threshold (*niṣāb*) for land produce, Imām Abū Ḥanīfah and Imām Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal held that the land-due applies to the harvest whether it is large or small.

Ibn Kathir adds a warning for those who harvest and give nothing: he points to the owners of the garden in Sūrat Nūn (68:17–33), who swore to pick their fruit at dawn, whispering to one another that no poor person would enter upon them that day — and woke to find the garden burnt black "like a pitch dark night," a punishment in this life with a greater one in the Hereafter.

## "And waste not — He does not love the wasteful"

The verse's closing prohibition of *isrāf* (extravagance, crossing proper limits) has drawn two readings, and Ibn Kathir gives both. The first ties it to excess even in giving: Ibn Jurayj related that it was revealed concerning Thābit bin Qays bin Shammās, who harvested his date-palms and resolved, "This day, every person who comes to me, I will feed him from it" — and kept feeding people until evening came and he had not a date left. The second, which Ibn Kathir prefers as the apparent meaning, connects it to the command "eat": do not waste in eating, "because this spoils the mind and the body" — exactly parallel to *"eat and drink but waste not by extravagance"* (7:31), and to the hadith which al-Bukhari recorded in his Sahih without a chain of narration: "Eat, drink and clothe yourselves without extravagance or arrogance."

Maʿārif answers the natural objection: how can spending in Allah's way ever be extravagance — could one ever give *enough*? Its answer is one of the passage's most practical insights: extravagance in one department of life causes shortfall in another. The one who empties his hands, even charitably, will fail the rights of his children, his family, his own self. So the rule is moderation even in the way of Allah, so that every due right is met.

## Ayah 142 — the herd

The cattle come "for burden and for *farsh*." ʿAbdullāh explained — in a report al-Ḥākim recorded, calling its chain Sahih — that the burden-animals are the camels that carry loads, and *farsh* the small camels. ʿAbdur-Raḥmān bin Zayd bin Aslam gave the broader reading Ibn Kathir judges sound: burden-animals are those people ride; *farsh* are those kept for meat and milk — like the sheep, too weak to carry anything, which gives you its meat and its wool for covers and mats. Ibn Kathir supports this from the Qur'an itself: the cattle subdued "so that some of them they have for riding and some they eat" (36:71–72), the "pure milk, palatable to the drinkers" drawn from between excretions and blood (16:66), and the wool, fur and hair made into furnishings and comfort (16:80).

Then comes this verse's own double command, spoken over the whole inventory: **"Eat of what Allah has provided for you"** — fruits, produce and cattle alike — **"and follow not the footsteps of Shaytan."** Ibn Kathir defines the footsteps: his way and his orders — precisely what the idolators followed when they prohibited what Allah had provided, "claiming that this falsehood came from Allah." Every food taboo invented without revelation is a step on his path. And the verse gives the reason: **"Surely he is to you an open enemy."** Ibn Kathir gathers the Qur'an's testimony — take him as an enemy, for he only invites his followers to the blazing Fire (35:6); he is the one who got your parents expelled from Paradise (7:27); what an evil exchange, to take him and his offspring as protectors instead of Allah (18:50). The pagans thought their taboos were piety; the Qur'an names their true lawgiver.

## Ayat 143–144 — the cross-examination

Now the argument sharpens into a courtroom scene. "Eight pairs" — Ibn ʿAbbās counts them as four pairs, male and female of each: sheep and goat in ayah 143, camel and ox in ayah 144 (compare 39:6, "He has sent down for you of cattle eight pairs"). Over each pair the same three questions are pressed: **Has He forbidden the two males?** Then every male would be unlawful. **Or the two females?** Then every female. **Or what the wombs of the two females enclose?** Then every newborn, whichever it was. Ibn ʿAbbās voices the divine logic: "Does the womb produce anything but males and females? So why do you prohibit some and allow some others?" The pagan rules cut across every category the animal kingdom actually contains — which proves they were drawn from nowhere. The wombs-question strikes their claim quoted in 6:139 head-on: "What is in the bellies of such-and-such cattle is for our males alone, and forbidden to our females."

**"Inform me with knowledge, if you are truthful"** — tell me, with real knowledge, how and when Allah prohibited the Baḥīrah, Sāʾibah, Waṣīlah and Ḥām. And if there is no transmitted knowledge: **"Or were you present when Allah ordered you this?"** Ibn Kathir notes the tone — Allah is mocking their innovations and their lies that He made sacred what they had forbidden. Religious law can rest only on revelation or on witnessed command; they had neither.

Then the verdict, one of the Qur'an's most severe: **"Who does more wrong than one who invents a lie against Allah to lead people astray without knowledge?"** No one, Ibn Kathir answers, is more unjust — and the person most worthy of this condemnation is ʿAmr bin Luḥayy bin Qumʿah, "the first person to change the religion of the Prophets" and designate the Sāʾibah, Waṣīlah and Ḥām, as mentioned in the Sahih. The customs of a whole civilisation traced back to one man's invention — and the passage closes over him and all who follow him: "Certainly Allah guides not the wrongdoing people."

## What the passage asks of a believer

Four threads run out of these ayat into a believer's life. **Lawfulness is the default** in what Allah created and provided; prohibition belongs to Him alone, and attributing man-made rules to Him is the gravest of lies. **Gratitude is the right response** to provision: as Maʿārif puts it, their duty was to remember the right of Allah whenever they benefited from His blessings, and to stop making satanic notions and inherited customs part of their faith. **Enjoyment and generosity travel together**: the same breath that says "eat" says "pay its due on the day of harvest" — provision arrives with the poor's share built into it. And **moderation guards both ends**: neither the hoarding of the garden's owners who shut out the poor, nor the self-ruinous excess of giving away one's last date; neither miserliness nor waste at the table.

passages.title: What Allah has actually forbidden to eat
passages.tafsir:
This passage is the Qur'an's decisive answer to man-made religion at the dinner table. The pagans of Makkah had hedged Allah's provision with invented prohibitions — and claimed, in Ibn Kathir's words, "this falsehood to be from Allah." In ayah 145 the Prophet ﷺ is commanded to sweep that system away with a single sentence: in all that has been revealed to me, only these few things are forbidden. Ayah 146 then recalls the far heavier restrictions once imposed on the Jews — imposed, the verse itself says, as recompense for their rebellion. And ayah 147 closes the file: if they still call you a liar, leave them between Allah's vast mercy and His unturnable judgment. What holds the three ayat together is one principle: **only Allah defines what is halal and what is haram — and His default is permission, not prohibition.**

## "Say: I do not find…" — the charter of lawful food (ayah 145)

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah commands His servant and Messenger, Muhammad ﷺ, to address "those who prohibited what Allah has provided them, claiming this falsehood to be from Allah." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene from the preceding verses: the Makkan disbelievers had taken their self-carved, lifeless idols as partners in the Divinity of Allah, made those idols "share" in the animals and blessings He alone had created, and given legal status to a whole body of ignorance-based, arbitrary customs. Into that thicket of invented rules comes the Prophet's ﷺ declaration.

Notice the wording: not "these things are forbidden," but *"I find not in that which has been revealed to me anything forbidden to be eaten by one who wishes to eat it, unless it be…"* The frame itself is an argument. The Prophet ﷺ speaks only from revelation; he searches what Allah has sent down and finds just four things:

1. **Maytah** — a dead animal.
2. **Blood poured forth** (*daman masfūḥan* — blood that is poured out).
3. **The flesh of swine** — "for that surely, is unclean (Rijs)."
4. What is **slaughtered in the name of other than Allah**.

Everything the idolators had added beyond this collapses. Ibn Kathir says this honorable ayah contradicts their innovated prohibitions for certain kinds of wealth, which rested "merely on their misguided ideas" — such as the *Baḥīrah*, *Sāʾibah*, *Waṣīlah* and *Ḥām*, the names they gave to types of animals they had declared off-limits on their own authority. Allah commanded His Messenger ﷺ to inform them that he does not find such animals prohibited in what Allah revealed to him. Whatever Allah did not prohibit here was left, in Ibn Kathir's phrase, "as that which does not have a ruling, i.e., permissible." And then the challenge is turned on them: how do you, O idolators, claim these things are prohibited, and why did you prohibit them when Allah did not prohibit them?

**The principle behind the verse.** Ibn Kathir records the statement of Ibn ʿAbbās — recorded by Abu Bakr bin Marduwyah and by Al-Hakim in his Mustadrak, who said, "Its chain is Sahih"; Abu Dawud also recorded it: "During the time of Jahiliyyah, the people used to eat some things and avoid some other things, because they disliked them. Later on, Allah sent His Prophet ﷺ, revealed His Book, allowed what He allowed, and prohibited what He prohibited. Therefore, whatever Allah allowed is lawful and whatever He prohibited is unlawful. Whatever He did not mention, there is no sin in it." He then recited this very ayah. This is the foundation the verse lays down: food is presumed lawful until Allah says otherwise. Prohibition needs revelation; permission needs nothing.

## The precision of "poured forth"

The qualifier on blood is doing real legal work. The verse does not forbid blood absolutely, but blood *poured forth*. Qatadah, quoted by Ibn Kathir, spells out the consequence: "Poured blood was prohibited, but the meat that still has some blood in it is allowed." A believer does not have to scrub every trace of redness from meat; the prohibition targets the poured blood, not the residue that clings to flesh. The Qur'an's restrictions are exact — and no wider than their wording.

## How far does "I find not" reach?

Ibn Kathir adds an important caution: the prohibited things mentioned in Surat Al-Ma'idah, and the hadiths on this subject, "amend the meaning of this Ayah" — the list here is not the whole of the law. He then relates an exchange that shows how seriously the companions took this verse's wording. ʿAmr bin Dinar told Jabir bin ʿAbdullah of the claim that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ prohibited the meat of donkeys at Khaybar. Jabir confirmed that Al-Hakam bin ʿAmr narrated that from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ — but "that scholar," Ibn ʿAbbās, denied it, and his answer was to recite this very ayah: *"I find not in that which has been revealed to me anything forbidden to be eaten by one who wishes to eat it…"* Al-Bukhari and Abu Dawud collected it. Whatever else is said on the question — and Ibn Kathir has already told us that later revelation and the hadiths amend this ayah — the exchange shows how firmly Ibn ʿAbbās held to its wording: for him, a prohibition had to be shown from revelation, never assumed.

## Sawdah's sheep — how precisely the Prophet ﷺ read this verse

Ibn Kathir brings a moving narration recorded by Imam Ahmad from Ibn ʿAbbās; Al-Bukhari and An-Nasa'i collected a similar hadith. A sheep belonging to Sawdah bint Zamʿah died, and she told the Prophet ﷺ. He asked, "Why did you not use its skin?" She said, "Should we use the skin of a sheep that has died?" Allah's Messenger ﷺ replied that Allah only said, *"I find not in that which has been revealed to me anything forbidden to be eaten by one who wishes to eat it, except Maytah (a dead animal) or blood poured forth, or the flesh of swine…"* — "You will not be eating it if you tan its skin and benefit from it." So she had the sheep skinned, and the skin was tanned and made into a water skin that she kept until it wore out.

Look at what the Prophet ﷺ is teaching her: the verse forbids the dead animal *to be eaten by one who wishes to eat it* — the prohibition attaches to eating, not to every conceivable use. Where the pagans multiplied taboos beyond revelation, the Prophet ﷺ refused to let even pious caution extend a prohibition one inch past its wording.

## The mercy clause: necessity

The ayah ends with a door held open: *"But whosoever is forced by necessity without willful disobedience, nor transgressing due limits; (for him) certainly, your Lord is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful."* Ibn Kathir says: whoever is forced by necessity to eat anything that Allah has forbidden in this honorable ayah, without transgressing his limits, then for him, certainly, your Lord is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful — and he notes that he explained this clause in Surat Al-Baqarah. Allah names Himself Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful precisely here, so that the one compelled to eat meets forgiveness, not condemnation.

## Ayah 146 — the heavier law given to the Jews, and why

Against this short list, ayah 146 sets what was once demanded of the Jews: *"And unto those who are Jews, We forbade every (animal) with undivided hoof, and We forbade them the fat of the ox and the sheep except what adheres to their backs or their Hawaya, or is mixed up with a bone."* Ibn Kathir explains the first clause: Allah forbade for the Jews every bird and animal with undivided hoof, such as the camel, ostrich, duck and goose. As for the fat: Ibn ʿAbbās, through ʿAli bin Abi Talhah, said "what adheres to their backs" refers to the fat that clings to their backs. The *ḥawāyā* are the entrails — so Abu Jaʿfar bin Jarir explained it, Ibn ʿAbbās said the same through ʿAli bin Abi Talhah, and similar was reported from Mujahid, Saʿid bin Jubayr and Ad-Dahhak. "Or is mixed up with a bone" means the fat mixed with bones remained lawful to them; Ibn Jurayj commented, "The fat on the rump that is mixed with the tailbone was allowed for them, and also the fat on the legs, head, eyes and what adheres to the bones," and As-Suddi said similarly.

Why such an intricate restriction? The verse answers itself: *"Thus We recompensed them for their rebellion. And verily, We are Truthful."* Ibn Kathir explains: We imposed this restriction on them as recompense for their rebellion and defying Our commandments — and he pairs the verse with Surat An-Nisa': *"For the wrongdoing of the Jews, We made unlawful for them certain good foods which had been lawful for them – and for their hindering many from Allah's way"* (4:160). And the closing oath — "We are Truthful" — answers a specific claim. As-Suddi mentioned that the Jews used to say these foods were things Israʼil — that is, Yaʿqub (peace be upon him) — had forbidden *for himself*, and they merely followed him. Ibn Jarir explains Allah's reply: We are Truthful in what We informed you of, O Muhammad ﷺ — it was Our forbidding of these foods for them, not, as they claimed, Israʼil's private abstention which they imitated. Allah was justified in the penalty He gave them.

Set beside ayah 145, the contrast is stark: the intricate prohibitions of ayah 146 were a penalty for rebellion, not a model of piety.

## Melting the fat: when law meets trickery

Ibn Kathir then records how that restriction was met with trickery — and the verdict of the Prophet ﷺ on it. ʿAbdullah bin ʿAbbās narrated that when ʿUmar bin Al-Khattab was told that Samurah sold liquor, he commented, "May Allah fight Samurah! Did he not know that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, *May Allah curse the Jews! The fats were forbidden for them, so they melted the fat and sold it.*" This hadith is recorded in the Two Sahihs. And Jabir bin ʿAbdullah said that in the year of the victory of Makkah he heard Allah's Messenger ﷺ saying: "Allah and His Messenger have forbidden selling alcoholic drinks (intoxicants), dead animals, swine and idols." He was asked, "What about the fat of dead animals? They are used to dye skins, paint ships and are used as light by the people." He said, "No, it is still unlawful," and then: "May Allah fight the Jews! When Allah forbade them the fats of animals, they melted the fat, sold it and ate its price." The collectors Ibn Kathir calls "the Group" recorded this hadith.

The lesson cuts deep. Changing a forbidden thing's *form* — melting the fat so it is no longer "fat," selling the thing rather than eating it, and consuming the price instead — does not change its *ruling*. Allah's prohibitions cannot be laundered through a loophole. ʿUmar applied the principle immediately to a Muslim selling wine: the curse that fell on those who played this game is a warning to this ummah, not a story about someone else.

## Ayah 147 — mercy wide open, judgment unturnable

What if, after all this, they still deny the Prophet ﷺ? Ayah 147 gives him his final word: *"Your Lord is the Owner of vast mercy, and never will His wrath be turned back from the people who are criminals."* Ibn Kathir reads the two halves as deliberate. If his opponents among the idolators, the Jews and their likes reject him, the first half encourages them to seek Allah's vast mercy and follow His Messenger ﷺ; the second discourages them from defying the Messenger, the Final Prophet, Muhammad ﷺ. He then observes that Allah often joins encouragement with threats in the Qur'an, and gathers the parallels — the end of this very surah, *"Surely, your Lord is swift in retribution, and certainly He is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful"* (6:165); *"But verily, your Lord is full of forgiveness for mankind in spite of their wrongdoing. And verily, your Lord is (also) severe in punishment"* (13:6); *"Declare unto My servants, that truly, I am the Oft-Forgiving, the Most Merciful. And that My torment is indeed the most painful torment"* (15:49–50); and the like in 40:3 and 85:12–14 — noting that there are many other ayat on this subject.

Neither half may be dropped. Mercy without warning breeds complacency; warning without mercy breeds despair. The deniers of the Prophet ﷺ are not met with an instant thunderbolt — the door of vast mercy stands open — but no one should mistake that patience for weakness, for when Allah's punishment comes for a people who persist in crime, nothing turns it back.

## Living it

Three things this passage asks of a believer. **First**, treat food the way Allah does: lawful until He says otherwise. Do not invent prohibitions in the name of piety, and do not accept "haram" from anyone who cannot show it in revelation — that was the sin of the Makkan idolators. **Second**, do not stretch prohibitions past their wording either — the Prophet ﷺ corrected even Sawdah's assumption that a dead sheep's skin could not be used. **Third**, never play the melting-the-fat game: renaming, reprocessing or reselling a forbidden thing to enjoy its benefit is the trick that earned a curse. And through it all, remember whom you are dealing with: a Lord whose mercy is vast enough to forgive the one forced by necessity to eat the forbidden — and whose judgment, once due, no one can turn away.

passages.title: The fatalist excuse 'had Allah willed' refuted
passages.tafsir:
This passage records a false notion the Makkan idolaters held about their shirk — an appeal to Allah's own will: "Had it been Allah's Will, we would not have associated partners with Him." Ibn Kathir presents ayat 148–150 as a debate: Allah mentions the idolators' argument, refutes it, and arms His Prophet ﷺ with three replies, each beginning with the command **qul** — "Say." Demand their evidence (ayah 148), declare that the perfect proof and argument belong to Allah (ayah 149), and summon their witnesses (ayah 150).

## The fatalist excuse — ayah 148

Ibn Kathir lays out their reasoning step by step. The idolaters said: surely Allah has full knowledge of the shirk we practise, and of the kinds of wealth we declare forbidden. He is able to change all of this — to direct us to faith and prevent us from disbelief. But He did not. Therefore, they concluded, Allah must have *willed, decided and agreed* that we do all this. In their mouths, the true doctrine that nothing happens outside Allah's will became a shield for idolatry.

Their claim covered two things at once: their **shirk** (associating partners with Allah) and their **invented prohibitions** — "nor would we have forbidden anything," which Ibn Kathir explains as their claim that "we forbid some kinds of wealth." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, in its commentary on the preceding verses of the sūrah, recalls how far astray the disbelievers of Makkah had gone: they took their self-carved, lifeless, insensate idols as partners in the Divinity of Allah, making them share in the animals He created and in many other blessings He had bestowed.
