They would set aside a portion of these blessings for Allah and another for their idols — then employ different excuses to move what belonged to Allah's portion into the portion reserved for the idols. Alongside this were many other ignorance-based arbitrary customs which they had given legal status.

Ibn Kathir notes that this was not a one-off argument. Allah records the same words from them elsewhere: "If it had been the will of the Most Gracious, we should not have worshipped them" (43:20), with a similar passage in Sūrah al-Naḥl.

## Why the argument fails

The ayah's own answer is history: "Likewise belied those who were before them — till they tasted Our wrath." Ibn Kathir explains: by using and relying on this very understanding, the misguided ones before them were led astray. And their ruin is itself the refutation. This notion, he writes, is false and ungrounded — for had it been true, Allah would not have harmed them, destroyed them, aided His honourable Messengers over them, and made them taste His painful punishment.

This is the fatal confusion at the heart of the fatalist excuse: it treats what Allah *allows to occur* as though it were what He is *pleased with*. The polytheists took His not-preventing them as His endorsement of them — and the fate of the earlier nations proves otherwise.

## Knowledge, conjecture, and guesswork

The first "Say" then goes for their evidence: "Have you any knowledge that you can produce before us?" Ibn Kathir glosses the demand precisely: any knowledge *that Allah is pleased with you and with your ways* — knowledge you can bring out and make "plain, apparent and clear for us." The verdict follows immediately: "You follow nothing but **ẓann**" — which Ibn Kathir explains as doubts and wishful thinking — "and you do nothing but lie" (**takhruṣūn**), uttering false claims about Allah with no basis at all.

The demand of this ayah is exacting: a claim about what Allah is pleased with requires **ʿilm** — real, producible knowledge — not conjecture dressed up as religion.

## The proof that reaches its mark — ayah 149

Now comes the turn of the passage: "Say: With Allah is **al-ḥujjah al-bālighah** — the perfect proof and argument; had He so willed, He would indeed have guided you all."

Notice what this ayah does *not* do. It does not deny that everything happens by Allah's will — it affirms it in almost the polytheists' own words: had He willed, He would have guided every one of you. But in Allah's mouth the sentence means the opposite of what it meant in theirs. Ibn Kathir explains the ḥujjah bālighah as Allah's "perfect wisdom and unequivocal proof to guide whom He wills and misguide whom He wills." The universal decree is *Allah's* argument — the proof of His sovereignty and wisdom — not the sinner's alibi.

Then Ibn Kathir states the balance in a single sentence: "All of this happens according to His decree, His will, and His choice. So in this way, He is pleased with the believers, and angry with the disbelievers." Both halves are affirmed together. Nothing — belief or disbelief — falls outside Allah's will; and yet His *pleasure* rests on the believers and His *anger* on the disbelievers. Will and pleasure are not the same thing, and the polytheists' whole argument depended on pretending they were.

Ibn Kathir gathers the sister-verses that state the same truth elsewhere in the Qur'an: "And had Allah willed, He could have gathered them together on true guidance" (6:35); "And had your Lord willed, those on earth would have believed, all of them together" (10:99); and the fullest statement: "And if your Lord had so willed, He could surely have made mankind one Ummah, but they will not cease to disagree — except him on whom your Lord has bestowed His mercy, and for that did He create them. And the Word of your Lord has been fulfilled: 'Surely, I shall fill Hell with jinns and men all together'" (11:118–119).

Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk compressed the whole ayah into one line: "No one has an excuse if he disobeys Allah. Surely, Allah has the perfect proof established against His servants." The decree explains *how* things happen; it never excuses the one who chose them.

## Bring your witnesses — ayah 150

The third "Say" moves from decree back to law. The polytheists had claimed not merely that Allah *permitted* their taboos, but that He had *forbidden* those things — which, Ibn Kathir says, "you have forbidden and lied and invented about Allah." Very well: "**Halumma shuhadāʾakum** — bring forward your witnesses who can testify that Allah has forbidden this." A claim about divine law is a testimony about Allah, and testimony demands witnesses.

Then comes a striking instruction: "If they do testify, do not testify with them." Ibn Kathir explains why: in that case their testimony is false and untrue. The Prophet ﷺ is commanded not to join a false testimony — falsehood confidently sworn to is still falsehood, and it is not to be met halfway.

The passage closes with a portrait of those whose desires must never be followed, marked by three traits: they belie Allah's ayat; they do not believe in the Hereafter; and "they hold others as equal with their Lord" — which Ibn Kathir explains as associating others with Allah in worship and treating them as His equals. The word "desires" (**ahwāʾ**) is the final diagnosis: strip away the theological-sounding argument about Allah's will, and what actually drove their religion was appetite — the wish to keep their shirk, their invented taboos, and the way of their fathers, exactly as the ayah's own words ("nor would our fathers") reveal.

## Living it

Aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk's principle is the enduring lesson: the divine decree is never a licence for disobedience. The argument of ayah 148 did not die in Makkah — the ayah itself says the nations before them belied in just the same way, till they tasted Allah's wrath. "If Allah didn't want me doing this, He would have stopped me" is that same ancient excuse, and this passage closes the door on it: Allah's will encompasses all things, and Allah's perfect proof stands against every sinner. The decree belongs to Him as the sign of His wisdom and sovereignty; it belongs to no one as a shield.

And ayah 150 adds the practical discipline that follows: claims about what Allah has forbidden require knowledge and truthful witness, not custom, conjecture, or confident assertion — and when falsehood is sworn to boldly, the believer's duty is to withhold agreement, not to split the difference.

passages.title: The commandments Allah has truly enjoined
passages.tafsir:
**These three ayat are the Qur'an's own "Ten Commandments" — a single summons in which Allah declares what He has truly prohibited, in ten commands spread across three verses, each verse sealed with its own refrain.** They arrive as a deliberate climax: for several sections before this, the sūrah has exposed how the pagan Arabs invented their own religion — declaring lawful what Allah forbade, forbidding what He allowed, even splitting foods between men and women by their own whim. Now the guesswork ends. As Ibn Kathir puts it, what the Prophet ﷺ recites here is "not guessing or wishful thinking. Rather, it is revelation and an order from Him."

## "Come" — the summons of ayah 151

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses on the very first word, *taʿālaw* ("Come!"). In Arabic this is what a caller says when he stands on high ground and calls those below to come **up** to him. The invitation itself carries a promise: accept it and you rise. And though the immediate audience was the idolaters of Makkah, al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ (cited in Maʿārif) notes the address is universal — believer and disbeliever, Arab and non-Arab, every generation to come.

## Why these verses are so honoured

The early Muslims treated this passage with extraordinary reverence:

- **The Prophet's ﷺ sealed will.** Ibn Masʿūd said: "Whoever wishes to read the will and testament of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on which he placed his seal, let him read these ayat" — from 151 to the end of 153 (recorded in Ibn Kathir).
- **A pledge of allegiance.** In al-Hakim's Mustadrak, ʿUbādah bin aṣ-Ṣāmit relates that the Prophet ﷺ asked, "Who among you will give me his pledge to do three things?" — then recited these ayat, promising that whoever fulfils the pledge, "his reward will be with Allah."
- **"The Mother of the Book."** Ibn ʿAbbās said that in Sūrat al-Anʿām "there are clear Ayat, and they are the Mother of the Book" (al-Hakim's Mustadrak), and elsewhere identified them as the *muḥkam* verses — those of firm, established meaning — mentioned in 3:7. Every prophet's religion, from Adam to Muhammad ﷺ, agreed on these commands; none was ever abrogated in any sharīʿah.
- Kaʿb al-Aḥbār, a scholar of the Torah before his Islam, said these ten prohibitions are what the Torah itself opens with.

Maʿārif also notes a subtlety of style: though the whole passage lists *prohibitions*, some are phrased as positive commands ("be good to parents") — meaning that acting against them is what is forbidden. The wisdom appears below.

## Ayah 151: the first five commands

**1. Never associate anything with Allah (shirk).** This heads the list because, as Maʿārif says, shirk is the one crime about which the Qur'an has given the decision that for it there is no forgiveness: "Verily, Allah forgives not (the sin of) setting up partners (in worship) with Him, but He forgives whom He wills, sins other than that" (4:116). The prohibition covers making idols into gods, calling prophets divine, taking angels as Allah's daughters — and, citing Tafsir Mazhari, it covers both **manifest** shirk (worshipping or obeying another as divine, or giving Allah's exclusive attributes of knowledge and power to prophets and saints) and **concealed** shirk: believing Allah is the Maker of all things yet, in practice, pinning all hopes on others — or worshipping correctly but to be seen, or giving charity for reputation. Shaykh Saʿdī captured it: to say "A made me gain and B made me lose" is itself a hidden shirk, for gain and loss come only from the Absolute Master.

Against this stands a door of immense hope. In the Two Sahihs — the collections of al-Bukhari and Muslim — Abū Dharr relates that Jibrīl gave the Prophet ﷺ the good news: "Whoever among your followers dies, worshipping none along with Allah, will enter Paradise." The Prophet ﷺ pressed him three times — "Even if he stole or committed illegal sexual intercourse?" — and each time the answer came: even then. And in a hadith recorded by some of the Musnad and Sunan compilers, the Prophet ﷺ related that Allah says: even if you brought the earth's fill of sins, "I will bring forth its fill of forgiveness, as long as you do not associate anything or anyone in worship with Me." Tawḥīd is the hinge on which everything else turns.

**2. Be good to parents.** Notice the phrasing: not "do not harm them" but *iḥsān* — active excellence. Maʿārif draws out the point: with parents it is not enough to avoid disobedience or pain; one's duty is to keep them *pleased* with generous, obliging treatment — what 17:24 expresses as "For them, lower your shoulders in humility." The Qur'an repeatedly couples duty to parents directly with worship of Allah Himself (17:23, 31:14) — this command sits second only to tawḥīd. In the Two Sahihs, Ibn Masʿūd asked the Prophet ﷺ which deed is best: "The prayer, when it is performed on time." Then? "Being dutiful to parents." Then? "Jihad in Allah's cause." And in Sahih Muslim, the Prophet ﷺ said three times, "Disgraced is he!" — the one who finds his parents (or one of them) in old age and still fails to enter Paradise through serving them. Maʿārif calls it an easy bargain: parents love their children by nature; a little kindness makes them happy — and old age is singled out because that is when service truly counts.

**3. Do not kill your children out of poverty.** The order of the passage is deliberate: after the right of parents comes the right of children (this is the thread the summary highlights). The Arabs of the Jāhiliyyah — the pre-Islamic days of ignorance in Arabia — buried daughters alive for fear of shame and sometimes killed sons for fear of want. The Qur'an treats the disease, not just the symptom: "**We** provide for you and for them." You are not the real provider — can a father make a seed split the earth and become a fruiting tree? Ibn Kathir notes the exquisite precision of the wording: here, where killing is driven by *present* poverty, Allah says "We provide for **you** and for them"; in 17:31, where it is *fear of future* poverty, He says "We provide for **them** and for you" — in each case putting first the one whose provision is in doubt. Maʿārif adds the hint: provision is given to parents *so that* they pass it to the weak — as the Prophet ﷺ taught, it is only for the sake of the weak among you that Allah helps and provides for you. Maʿārif then presses a sobering modern application: parents who neglect their children's religious upbringing, leaving them dead to Allah and the Ākhirah, commit a kind of killing too — one that ruins not a transitory life but an eternal one. In the Two Sahihs, when Ibn Masʿūd asked which sin is greatest, the Prophet ﷺ answered: to call a rival for Allah, while He alone created you — then, "to kill your son for fear that he might share your food."

**4. Do not even come near shameful deeds, open or secret.** *Al-fawāḥish* (singular *fāḥishah*) denotes, in Qur'anic usage, every evil whose corrupting effects spread far and wide — most commonly acts of indecency. The commentators (as Maʿārif surveys) read "open and secret" in complementary ways: sins of the limbs versus sins of the heart (envy, malice, greed); or public immorality versus secret scheming; or sins everyone recognises versus those people don't realise are ḥarām. All agree on the force of *lā taqrabū* — "do not **approach**": avoid not just the sin but its preliminaries, places, and pathways, for as the Prophet ﷺ warned, it is not unlikely that one who keeps roaming around a prohibited place will enter it as well. Behind the prohibition stands something awesome about Allah Himself: in the Two Sahihs the Prophet ﷺ said, "None is more jealous than Allah. This is why He has forbidden the immoral sins committed openly or secretly" — words he repeated when Saʿd bin ʿUbādah swore he would kill with the sword any man he found with his wife: "Do you wonder at Saʿd's jealousy? By Allah, I am more jealous than Saʿd, and Allah is more jealous than I." The "jealousy" here is the fierce protectiveness of honour that Saʿd's oath displays — and the hadith itself declares Allah's to be above the Prophet's ﷺ, as his is above Saʿd's.

**5. Do not kill any soul Allah has made sacred, except by right.** Though already included under fawāḥish, it is singled out for emphasis. The "just cause" is defined by the Prophet ﷺ himself in the Two Sahihs: a Muslim's blood is lawful only for three — the married adulterer, a life for a life (qiṣāṣ), and the apostate who abandons the community. Maʿārif recounts that ʿUthmān, besieged by rebels, recited this very ḥadīth to them: "With the grace of Allah, I have been free of these things all my life... Then, on what basis do you want to kill me?" And the sanctity extends beyond Muslims: in al-Bukhari the Prophet ﷺ said that whoever kills a *muʿāhid* — a non-Muslim under treaty of protection — "shall not smell the scent of Paradise, though its scent is perceived from a distance of forty years" (and in the narration of Abū Hurayrah recorded by Ibn Majah and at-Tirmidhi — at-Tirmidhi grading it "Hasan Sahih" — seventy years).

The verse closes: *"This He has commanded you, that you may **understand** (taʿqilūn)."*

## Ayah 152: four more commands

**6. The orphan's wealth — approach it only "with that which is best."** Guardians must treat an orphan's property, Maʿārif says, as if it were fire — yet protecting and profitably investing it is not merely allowed but required. When this ayah and 4:10 came down, the Companions so feared mixing with orphans' property that they separated even food and drink, letting leftovers spoil rather than touch them — until Allah revealed 2:220, "The best thing is to work honestly in their property... they are your brothers" (Ibn ʿAbbās's account, collected by Abu Dawud). Guardianship ends when the orphan "attains full strength" (*ashudd*) — adolescence, according to ash-Shaʿbī, Mālik and others of the Salaf. Maʿārif adds the fiqh: maturity alone is not enough; per 4:6 the youth must also show *rushd*, the ability to manage wealth — the guardian holding it, if need be, up to age twenty-five, after which (in Abū Ḥanīfah's view) it is handed over regardless, while other Imams held a judge should appoint a trustee.

**7. Give full measure and full weight, with justice.** Allah destroyed an entire nation for cheating the scales, and Sūrat al-Muṭaffifīn (83:1–6) pronounces "woe" on those who demand full measure when receiving but give short when paying — asking, do they not think they will be resurrected for a Great Day? Maʿārif widens the lens brilliantly: *taṭfīf* (short-changing) is not confined to scales. In Mālik's Muwaṭṭaʼ, ʿUmar saw a man making the required movements of his prayer short and said, "You made taṭfīf" — and Imam Mālik comments that full measure and short measure apply to *everything*. The employee who steals time, the worker who under-delivers, the official or scholar who falls short of his duty — all fall under "al-muṭaffifīn." The verse immediately adds, "We burden not any soul beyond its capacity": one who strives honestly is excused an inadvertent slip. Better still is generosity beyond the due — the Prophet ﷺ told a weigher, "Weigh, and tilt the balance" in the receiver's favour (Ahmad, Abu Dawud, Tirmidhi), and said, in al-Bukhari's narration from Jābir, may Allah's mercy be on the one who is lenient when selling and when collecting.

**8. When you speak, be just — even against a relative.** Nothing is specified, so the majority of commentators take it comprehensively: testimony, judgment, and everyday speech must all meet the standard of truth — with no word added or subtracted, whomever it helps or harms, and neither love nor enmity bending it (as 4:135 and 5:8 command explicitly). The stakes are severe: the Prophet ﷺ said three times, "False witness is equal to shirk" (Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah), and taught that of three kinds of judges, one goes to Paradise — the one who found the truth and ruled by it — while the judge who knew the truth and ruled against it, and the one who ruled in ignorance, both go to the Fire (Abu Dawud).

**9. Fulfil the covenant of Allah.** Ibn Jarir explains it as obeying what Allah commanded, refraining from what He prohibited, and abiding by His Book and His Messenger's ﷺ Sunnah. Maʿārif offers that it may mean the primordial pledge — when Allah asked every soul, "Am I not your Lord?" and all replied, "Yes indeed" — or the specific pledges in the Qur'an, including these very verses; the scholars include vows (*nadhr*) made to Allah. Ninth in the list, yet in reality this command encompasses the whole sharīʿah.

This verse closes: *"...that you may **remember** (tadhakkarūn)."*

## Ayah 153: the tenth command — one straight path

"**This is My path, perfectly straight — so follow it, and do not follow the other ways, for they will separate you from His way.**" "This" means the religion of Islam, or the Qur'an — possibly Sūrat al-Anʿām itself, since it contains the whole framework of the faith (Maʿārif). And note the grammar Ibn Kathir highlights: Allah's path is *singular*, because truth is one; the other ways are *plural*, because misguidance is many and divided. This tenth command entrusts the entire field of lawful and unlawful to the Prophet's ﷺ sharīʿah — no one may go about deciding ḥalāl and ḥarām on his own, which was precisely the crime of the Jāhiliyyah this passage came to end.

The Prophet ﷺ made it visible. Imam Ahmad records from Ibn Masʿūd (al-Hakim: "its chain is Sahih") that he drew a line in the sand: "This is Allah's path, leading straight." Then lines to its right and left: "These are the other paths, on each path there is a devil who calls to it," and he recited this ayah. Ibn Masʿūd later described the straight path, in a report recorded by Ibn Jarir: "Muhammad ﷺ left us at its lower end and its other end is in Paradise" — with callers on the side-paths, and whoever follows them ends in the Fire. And in the parable of an-Nawwās bin Samʿān (Imam Ahmad; also recorded by at-Tirmidhi and an-Nasa'i, at-Tirmidhi saying "Hasan Gharib"): the path runs between two walls with open doors curtained over — the path is Islam, the walls Allah's limits, the doors His prohibitions, the caller at its gate the Qur'an, and the caller from above it "Allah's admonition in the heart of every Muslim." Ibn ʿAbbās read the verse alongside 42:13 as Allah's command to hold to the Jamāʿah — the united community — for the nations before were destroyed by division. Tafsir Mazhari adds a piercing diagnosis: the side-paths begin wherever people, instead of moulding their lives to the Qur'an and Sunnah, mould the Qur'an and Sunnah to their own desires by convenient "interpretation."

## Three refrains, one ascending ladder

Maʿārif ends with a gem. Each verse closes differently, and the sequence is deliberate. The first five prohibitions end with *"that you may understand"* — because the people of the Jāhiliyyah saw nothing wrong in shirk or burying daughters; only awakened **reason** could break blind custom. The next four end with *"that you may remember"* — for even the pagans knew orphans, fair scales and honest speech mattered; their failure was heedlessness, and its cure is remembrance. The final command ends with *"that you may have **taqwā**"* — fear and consciousness of Allah — because nothing but taqwā can hold a person on the straight path against the pull of his own desires. Reason recognises the truth; remembrance keeps it present; taqwā makes you live it. And at all three seals stands the word *waṣṣākum* — "He has enjoined this upon you" — the very language of a *waṣiyyah*, a will. Which is why the Companions said: whoever wishes to see the sealed testament of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, let him recite these three verses.

passages.title: Moses' Scripture and this blessed Book remove excuses
passages.tafsir:
# The Two Books That Close Every Door of Excuse

This passage brings the great closing argument of Sūrat al-Anʿām to its point of no return. Having just declared, "And verily, this is My straight path, so follow it" (ayah 153), Allah now sets two Scriptures side by side — the Tawrah given to Mūsā (ayah 154) and "this blessed Book," the Qur'an (ayah 155) — and then names two excuses that might one day have been pleaded (ayat 156–157), refuting both before they could ever be spoken. Ibn Kathir treats the passage in two movements, and his two headings mark them: the first pair of ayat he discusses under **"Praising the Tawrah and the Qur'an,"** and the excuses under **"The Qur'an is Allah's Proof Against His Creation."** Praise first, then proof — and once this Book has come, no one can plead ignorance.

## Why the Tawrah appears here

It may seem abrupt that, after praising the Qur'an as the straight path, ayah 154 suddenly turns to Mūsā. Ibn Kathir explains that this is a deliberate pairing: Allah **often mentions the Qur'an and the Tawrah together**. He gathers the evidence — "And before this was the Scripture of Mūsā as a guide and a mercy. And this is a confirming Book in the Arabic language" (46:12); earlier in this very sūrah, "Say: Who then sent down the Book which Mūsā brought, a light and a guidance to mankind…?" (6:91), followed at once by "And this is a blessed Book which We have sent down" (6:92); the idolators' complaint, "Why is he not given the like of what was given to Mūsā?" — to which Allah replied, "Did they not disbelieve in that which was given to Mūsā of old?", for they had called the two Books "two kinds of magic, each helping the other" and declared, "Verily, in both we are disbelievers" (28:48); and the jinn who said, "We have heard a Book sent down after Mūsā, confirming what came before it, it guides to the truth" (46:30).

The point is that the two revelations stand or fall together. The same Lord who gave Mūsā a complete Scripture has now sent down its confirmation in Arabic — so the Makkans cannot honour the one in theory while rejecting the other in practice.

## "Complete for that which is best"

The phrase in ayah 154, *tamāman ʿalā alladhī aḥsan* — "complete for that which is best" — carries two layers, and Ibn Kathir opens both.

First, **completeness of the Book itself**: "We made the Book that We revealed to Mūsā a complete and comprehensive Book, sufficient for what he needs to complete his Law." He compares it to "And We wrote for him on the Tablets the lesson to be drawn from all things" (7:145). The Tawrah was not a fragment; it was a full charter for its people — "explaining all things in detail, and a guidance and a mercy."

Second, **completion as a reward for excellence**: *ʿalā alladhī aḥsan* means, in Ibn Kathir's words, "as a reward for his doing right and obeying Our commands and orders." Mūsā's own doing of what is best was met with Allah's completing favour. Ibn Kathir sets this in a wider Qur'anic pattern: "Is there any reward for good other than what is best?" (55:60); Ibrāhīm, who fulfilled his Lord's commands and was made "an Imam for mankind" (2:124); and the leaders raised from the Children of Israel "when they were patient and believed with certainty in Our Ayat" (32:24). The rule running through all of these: Allah entrusts guidance to those who prove themselves in obedience.

And the aim of the whole gift, the ayah says, was "that they might believe in the meeting with their Lord" — Scripture exists to prepare people for standing before Allah.

## The blessed Book, and what it asks of us

Ayah 155 turns from the past to the present: "And this is a blessed Book (the Qur'an) which We have sent down, so follow it and have Taqwa, so that you may receive mercy."

Ibn Kathir reads this ayah as an open summons: Allah "encourages His servants to follow His Book, and orders them to **understand it, adhere to it, and call to it**." Note the sequence — not mere recitation, but comprehension, then obedience, then inviting others. And the Book is called *mubārak*, blessed, "for those who follow and implement it in this life and the Hereafter, because it is the **Firm Rope of Allah**." The blessing, in other words, is not automatic; it flows to the one who takes hold of the rope. The ayah's own grammar makes the same point: follow it and have taqwā, *so that* you may receive mercy.

## The two excuses, named and cancelled

Ayat 156–157 are remarkable: Allah quotes objections that had not yet been raised, in order to strip them of all force in advance.

**The first excuse (ayah 156):** "The Book was sent down only to two sects before us, and for our part, we were in fact unaware of what they studied." The "two sects," Ibn Kathir reports, are the Jews and the Christians — this is the explanation narrated by ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah from Ibn ʿAbbās, and similar was reported from Mujāhid, As-Suddī, Qatādah and several others. The imagined plea runs: revelation came in a foreign tongue to foreign peoples; "we did not understand what they said because the revelation was not in our tongue. We, indeed, were busy and unaware of their message." Ibn Jarir explains the logic of the ayah: this Book was sent down precisely "so that you do not say" this — "this way, you will have no excuse." He connects it to 28:47: had a calamity struck them first for what their hands sent forth, they would have said, "Our Lord! Why did You not send us a Messenger? We would then have followed Your Ayat." Allah's justice forecloses that protest by sending the Messenger before the reckoning.

**The second excuse (ayah 157):** "If only the Book had been sent down to us, we would surely have been better guided than they." Ibn Kathir explains the sense: "We also refuted this excuse, had you used it" — lest they say, "If a Book was revealed to us, just as they received a Book, we would have been better guided than they are." And he sets beside it a parallel ayah: "And they swore by Allah their most binding oath that if a warner came to them, they would be more guided than any of the nations (before them)" (35:42). Both escape routes are now sealed with one sentence: "So now has come unto you a clear proof from your Lord, and a guidance and a mercy." Ibn Kathir unpacks the three terms: a Glorious Qur'an revealed to Muhammad ﷺ, the Arab Prophet — so the plea that "the revelation was not in our tongue" can never be spoken again — containing "the explanation of the lawful and unlawful matters, guidance for the hearts, and mercy from Allah to His servants who follow and implement it."

## Was the earlier ignorance real? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's discussion

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses over that first excuse with a careful question: how could the Arabs truly have been "unaware of what they studied," when a scripture's contents can always reach people through translation? His answer: the ignorance was real, but its cause lay with the People of the Book, who "never took steps to educate and inform the people of Arabia" in the teachings of monotheism. What the Arabs caught of scripture was only what "falls within hearing distance casually" — and such stray hearing "is customarily ineffective as a meaningful warning." It was, however, enough to make searching and reflection obligatory, so that punishment for abandoning Tauhīd (the belief in the Oneness of Allah) would still have been possible even before the Qur'an.

He then guards against a misreading: none of this casts doubt on the universal nature of the prophetic missions of Mūsā and ʿĪsā, peace be upon them. In the fundamentals of faith, following all prophets is obligatory on all peoples; what is unique to our master ﷺ is that his message is universal "in terms of the totality of fundamentals and subsidiaries" — every detail, for everyone. So even before the Qur'an the excuse was thin; "now that too is no more valid. **The argument of Allah is already established.**"

As for the second excuse, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes it touches the question of salvation during the *fatrah* — the gap between prophets when no fresh revelation was present — a matter he treats under verse 19 of Sūrat al-Māʼidah.

## The gravest wrong: *ṣadafa*

With the excuses gone, ayah 157 closes with a verdict: "Who then does more wrong than one who rejects the Ayat of Allah and *ṣadafa* away therefrom?" Ibn Kathir records a genuine difference among the early authorities over this rare verb. **As-Suddī** explained *ṣadafa* as active obstruction: such a person "discouraged and hindered people from following" the Ayat of Allah. **Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and Qatādah** said it means simply that he "turned away from it." On either reading, the person described is one who "neither benefited from what the Messenger ﷺ brought, nor followed what he was sent with by abandoning all other ways" — and the ayah's warning falls on him: "We shall requite those who turn away from Our Ayat with an evil torment, because of their turning away." The punishment is stated as the precise consequence of the turning away itself — measure for measure.

## Living it

The passage leaves the believer with no neutral ground. The excuses of a foreign tongue, of being "busy and unaware," and of "if only" belonged to a world before the Qur'an; they no longer exist. What remains is exactly what ayah 155 commands and Ibn Kathir spells out: follow this Book, understand it, adhere to it, and call others to it — holding fast to it as the Firm Rope of Allah, in hope of the mercy the ayah promises.

passages.title: Waiting for the Hour when faith is useless
passages.tafsir:
Sūrah al-Anʿām has spent its length dismantling the case of the Makkan disbelievers — answering their questions, correcting their beliefs, setting Allah's signs before their eyes. As Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān observes, by this point the avenues of truth lay open and the argument of Allah stood conclusively established against them; believing was all that remained. So this closing passage asks the only question left: **what exactly are you waiting for?** Ayah 158 names the deadline — the moment the unseen becomes seen and the door of faith swings shut. Ayah 159 marks out the one road to walk before that moment, disowning every splintering away from it. Ayah 160 then discloses the terms of the final accounting — terms so tilted toward mercy that delay becomes indefensible. Deadline, road, reckoning: the three stand together as the sūrah's final warning and its final invitation.

## What is left to wait for? — ayah 158

Ibn Kathir reads the verse as a stern threat to those who defy Allah's Messengers, deny His signs and block His path. Three things are named as the only events these people could still be "waiting" for, and Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān unfolds them: are they waiting to believe only when the angels of death actually reach them? Or when they stand on the plain of Resurrection and their Lord Himself comes to decide destinies? Or when the last signs heralding the Day of Judgment finally appear? Each is a moment when believing costs nothing — and counts for nothing.

**"Or your Lord should come."** The Qur'an affirms in several places that Allah will come on the Day of Judgment — Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān cites the parallel in 2:210, "that Allah comes upon them in canopies of clouds with the angels." How this will be cannot be conceived by human imagination, and here Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān states what it calls the standard creed of the noble Companions and the righteous elders of this Ummah: believe in what has been mentioned in the Qur'an, have faith in it, and resign the matter of *how* it shall come to pass to Divine knowledge. One is simply certain that Allah will be present on the Day of Judgment — without having to worry about the state and orientation in which this would happen.

## The sun from the west

The Qur'an deliberately says only "some of the signs of your Lord" without naming them. The Prophet ﷺ named the decisive one. In a hadith recorded by al-Bukhari from Abu Hurayrah, he ﷺ said: "The Last Hour will not commence until the sun rises from the west. When the people witness that, they will all believe. This is when *no good will it do a person to believe then, if he believed not before*." Ibn Jarir recorded, also from Abu Hurayrah, that three things close the door once they appear: the sun rising from its west, the Dajjāl (the great end-times deceiver), and the Beast of the earth — and in Ahmad's narration the Smoke is added.

Ibn Kathir preserves a vivid scene behind this. Three men in Madinah heard Marwan declare that the first sign would be the Dajjāl. They took it to the Companion 'Abdullah bin 'Amr, who replied that Marwan had said nothing; he himself had heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say that the first of the signs to appear are the sun rising from the west and the Beast emerging in the early morning — whichever comes first, the other follows on its heels. Then 'Abdullah described the sun's nightly journey: it passes beneath the Throne, prostrates, and seeks permission to return, and is permitted — until the night Allah wills otherwise. It seeks leave and receives no answer; again, and no answer; until it realises that even if permitted it could no longer reach the east in time. "My Lord! The east is so far — what good would I be to the people?" At last it is told: *Rise from your place* — and it rises upon mankind from where it set. Ibn Kathir notes this was recorded by Imam Ahmad, and also by Muslim in his Sahih and by Abu Dawud and Ibn Majah in their Sunans.

Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān adds the wider map from Sahih Muslim, narrated by Hudhayfah ibn Usayd: the Hour will not come until ten signs have been seen — the sun rising from the west, the Smoke, the Beast of the earth, Gog and Magog, the coming of ʿĪsā (peace be upon him), the Dajjāl, three sinkings of the land (in the east, the west, and Arabia), and a fire emerging from Eden driving people before it. And in the Musnad of Ahmad, from Ibn 'Umar: the first of these to emerge will be the sun from the west and the Beast.

A subtle point of wording, noted in Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān: the phrase "some signs of your Lord" is repeated in the ayah without a pronoun — "or that *some signs of your Lord* come; the day *some signs of your Lord* come, believing will not benefit…" This hints that the two sets of signs are not identical: many portents will come, but a particular final sign — the sun's rising, on the Prophet's ﷺ explanation — is the one that seals the door.

## Why faith will not count then

Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān gives the underlying reason. Iman (faith) and tawbah (repentance) are accepted only so long as they remain a *choice*. Once divine punishment and the reality of the next life become open to plain perception, every human being is compelled to believe — and faith under duress, repentance under threat, is not faith at all. This is why the people of Hell who beg to be returned are told, in effect: the time for belief and deed is over; what you say now, you say because you have no other option. Ibn Kathir cites the same principle from the Qur'an itself: "when it is upon them, how can they benefit then by their reminder?" (47:18), and "then their faith could not avail them when they saw Our punishment" (40:84–85).

Ibn Kathir is precise about who loses what. The disbeliever who believes only then — it is not accepted. The believer who had already earned good — his prior good stands to his credit. But the believer who had neither done good nor repented before that day finds that new deeds and new repentance are no longer received.

One difficulty is raised in Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān: authentic reports say that when ʿĪsā (peace be upon him) returns, he will call people to faith and they will believe — how, if faith has become unacceptable? Alusi answers in Ruh al-Maʿani that the sun's rising will occur long after ʿĪsā's era, and only then does the door close. 'Allamah Balqini and others suggested the bar may not even remain in force through that entire last period. The scholars differed, and Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān leaves it with: Allah knows best.

## Every death is a private Last Hour

Why did the Qur'an itself leave the sign unnamed? Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān cites al-Bahr al-Muhit: the very ambiguity keeps heedless people on alert, so that every ominous event drives them to repent and correct course *now*. And the brevity carries a second warning: what happens cosmically when the sun rises from the west happens in miniature for every individual at death. The Qur'an says it plainly: "Tawbah is not accepted from those who keep committing sins until death visits one of them and he says, 'Now I repent'" (4:18). The Prophet ﷺ explained that a servant's repentance goes on being accepted until the *ghargharah* — the rattle when the soul reaches the throat and the angels of death come into view. Some scholars, as reported in al-Bahr al-Muhit, put it in a sentence: *whoever dies, his Qiyamah has already dawned* — the time of deeds is over, and from the grave onward he begins to see a sample of what awaits. The Persian poet Sa'ib compressed it into a line: repentance after the last breath stands rejected — "unaware man, you are late; the door of the beloved is closed."

Hence the ayah's ending: "Say: Wait then — we too are waiting." Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān paraphrases: if, after all the arguments, they still prefer to wait for death or the Day of Doom, they are welcome to wait; we shall be waiting to see what their Lord decides to do with them. Ibn Kathir calls it a stern threat — and a sure promise.

## One religion, many splinters — ayah 159

If ayah 158 is the deadline, ayah 159 is the road that must be kept until then. Mujahid, Qatadah, Ad-Dahhak and As-Suddi said the verse came down about the Jews and Christians, who — as Ibn 'Abbas explained — had already disputed and broken into sects before the Prophet ﷺ was sent. But Ibn Kathir holds that its apparent wording is general: it covers everyone who defies the religion of Allah or deserts it. Allah's law is one and contains no contradiction; a hadith Ibn Kathir cites has the Prophet ﷺ say that the Prophets are half-brothers with one religion. The straight path all the Messengers brought is worship of Allah alone and adherence to the law of the final Messenger ﷺ; every other path is misguidance, opinion and desire — and Allah declared His Messenger ﷺ free of them all: "you have no concern with them in the least." Their case rests with Allah, "Who then will tell them what they used to do."

Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān distinguishes two kinds of straying. Some ways of error run in the *opposite* direction to the straight path — outright disbelief and idolatry. Others do not reverse course entirely but pull the traveller off to the right and left: the ways of *shubuhāt* (doubts sown into settled faith) and *bidʿah* (innovation — adding to the religion what is not from it, or dropping what is). Tafsir Mazhari includes under this verse both the past communities who corrupted their religion and the innovators of this Ummah who keep adding baseless things to Islam.

The Prophet ﷺ foretold exactly this. In the narration of Ibn 'Umar reported by Tirmidhi and Abu Dawud: the Bani Isra'il split into seventy-two sects; my Ummah will split into seventy-three, all in the Fire except one. Asked which, he ﷺ said: *that upon which I and my Companions are.* Al-Tabarani reports on sound authority from Sayyidna Faruq al-A'zam — the title of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him — that he told Sayyidah 'A'ishah that the sects of this very verse are the people of bidʿah, who invent new ways in religion out of their own desires — and the like is soundly reported from Abu Hurayrah. And in the hadith of Al-'Irbad ibn Sariyah, reported by Imam Ahmad, Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi, the Prophet ﷺ ordered: those who live after me will see many differences — so hold fast to my Sunnah and the Sunnah of the rightly-guided caliphs, and beware of newly invented methods, for everything introduced anew into the religion is bidʿah, and every bidʿah is straying.

Why are the Companions the criterion? Tafsir Mazhari explains that "the Jamaʿah" — the body one must not leave, for the Prophet ﷺ warned (in a hadith in Abu Dawud and Ahmad) that whoever separates from it even a hand-span has slipped the band of Islam's allegiance from his neck — means the Companions. Allah promised to explain the Qur'an through His Messenger ﷺ ("then, to make it clear is on Us" — 75:19); the Prophet ﷺ trained the Companions in that explanation by word and deed; so their collective understanding *is* the authoritative exposition of the Shariʿah. The believer's good fortune is to follow the Book and the Sunnah, and wherever doubt arises over a verse or hadith, to take the meaning the Companions preferred. The sects arose, Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān says, precisely when people set that rule aside and read their own wishes into revelation.

## Tenfold — and more: ayah 160

Ayah 159 ended with the affair resting with Allah, "Who then will tell them what they used to do." Ayah 160 now discloses how that telling is weighted: whoever comes with a good deed receives ten times its like; whoever comes with an evil deed is repaid only its equal — "and they shall not be wronged." Ibn Kathir notes it makes specific the general promise of 28:84, "whoever comes with good will receive better than that."

The hadith recorded by Imam Ahmad from Ibn 'Abbas — also in al-Bukhari, Muslim and an-Nasa'i — opens the ledger fully. The Prophet ﷺ said of his Lord: "Your Lord is Most Merciful. Whoever intends a good deed and does not do it, it is written for him as a good deed. If he does it, it is written as ten, up to seven hundred, up to many times more. Whoever intends an evil deed and does not do it, it is written for him as a good deed. If he does it, it is written as one sin — unless Allah erases it. Only those who deserve destruction will be destroyed by Allah." Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān closes the report with a conclusion it takes from Ibn Kathir: with grace and mercy showering like this in the presence of Allah, who can apprehend total destruction — unless there be that rare person who is determined to be destroyed?

Ibn Kathir refines the point about abandoned sins: the one who leaves a sin *fearing Allah* earns a good deed — in some narrations of the Sahih, Allah says "he has left the sin for My sake"; the one who simply forgets or is distracted earns neither reward nor sin; but the one who abandons it only through inability or laziness, after chasing the means to commit it, is like the one who committed it — as in the authentic hadith of the two Muslims who meet with drawn swords: killer and killed are both in the Fire, for the slain man "was eager to kill his companion."

Then comes the *hadith qudsi* — a hadith in which the Prophet ﷺ relates words from his Lord — narrated by Abu Dharr and recorded by Ahmad and Muslim: "Whoever performs a good deed will have tenfold for it, and more. Whoever commits a sin, his recompense is its like — unless I forgive. Whoever commits the earth's fill of sins and then meets Me associating nothing with Me, I will give him its fill of forgiveness. Whoever draws closer to Me by a hand's span, I draw closer to him by a forearm; whoever draws closer by a forearm, I draw closer by an arm's length. And whoever comes to Me walking, I come to him running." Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān points out that the verse's "tenfold" is therefore a floor, not a ceiling — other narrations carry it to seventy and seven hundred times.

Ibn Kathir shows this arithmetic at work in worship: at-Tabarani reports from Abu Malik al-Ash'ari that one Friday prayer to the next erases what lies between them plus three more days — *because* Allah says "whoever brings a good deed shall have ten times the like thereof"; and in the hadith of Abu Dharr recorded by Ahmad, an-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah, fasting three days of every month equals fasting all the time — Tirmidhi's version (which he graded hasan) adds that Allah sent down this very ayah in affirmation: a day earns ten days.

**"Whoever comes with a good deed."** Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān, citing al-Bahr al-Muhit, dwells on the choice of verb: the ayah does not say whoever *does* a good deed but whoever *comes with* one — brings it, intact, to the meeting with Allah. A deed must survive to the end to be rewarded. Shirk and kufr destroy all good deeds; lesser sins can spoil particular ones — "do not nullify your charities by boasting about favour and by teasing" (2:264) — and it appears in hadith that worldly chatter in the masjid eats up good deeds as fire eats wood. The mercy cuts the other way for sins: repented from, a sin is erased and never has to be "brought" at all. So the decisive question is not what you once did but what you arrive with — and the method, Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān says, is to keep repenting and seeking Allah's forgiveness so the good survives and the evil does not. "And they shall not be wronged": this is no human court; no one's reward will be shaved down, no one's punishment inflated.

Read together, the three ayat leave the believer with a single posture. Do not wait — the door of faith and tawbah is open now, and only now, and no one knows which morning the sun will rise wrongly or which breath will reach the throat. Keep to the one road, measured by the way of the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions, refusing the pull of sects and inventions to the right and left. And walk toward a Lord whose scales are weighted for you, not against you — who writes ten for one, who forgives the earth's fill of sins to the one who meets Him associating nothing with Him, and who comes running to the one who comes walking.

passages.title: My life and death are for Allah alone
passages.tafsir:
These are the closing verses of Sūrah al-Anʿām, and they gather the whole sūrah into a single declaration. After chapter-long arguments against shirk (associating partners with Allah) and a portrait of people who had altered the true religion and split into factions, the Prophet ﷺ is now commanded — three times with the word *qul*, "Say" — to announce his own creed aloud: the path he stands on (161), the total dedication of his worship, life and death to Allah (162–163), and his refusal to take any lord besides Allah (164). The passage then closes, and the sūrah with it, on Allah's verdict over history: He makes generations succeed one another on the earth as a test, and He is both swift in punishment and Most-Forgiving, Very-Merciful (165). Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān notes that the first three of these verses present an "authentic profile" of the true religion — the first two carrying its fundamental principle, the third its subsidiaries — set against the fragmented religion of those who had corrupted it.

## The straight path, and why Ibrahim is named (161)

**"My Lord has guided me."** The wording carries a quiet argument. Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān points out the hint: the Prophet ﷺ has not arrived at this path through his own ideas or under the weight of ancestral custom — the very things that held his opponents in place. He was *directed to it by his Lord*. And the choice of the word *Rabb* matters: it names Allah as the essential nurturer, benefactor and carer in all conditions — a meaning, Maʿārif observes, that no single English word captures. Guiding to the right path is the very dictate of that care: whoever looks for guidance will have it from Him.

**"A right religion" — dīnan qiyaman.** The word *qiyam* is a verbal noun meaning that which stands established on strong, secure foundations. This religion is fortified; it rests on what Allah sent down, not on anyone's personal ideas. Nor is it a strange new religion raising doubting eyebrows — it has been the religion of all the prophets before.

**Why "the religion of Ibrahim"?** Because, Maʿārif explains, every group of that time — the Jews, the Christians, and the disbelievers of Arabia, however much they differed — was unanimous in paying homage to the great spiritual station of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and each sect claimed to be his true adherents. This verse removes the misgiving. Ibrahim's defining achievement was that he never bowed to anyone other than Allah and had a distaste for every form of shirk — he was *ḥanīf*, upright in pure monotheism. Meanwhile his claimants were soaked in shirk: the Jews with ʿUzayr, the Christians with ʿIsa, and the disbelievers of Arabia took thousands of rocks as partners in Allah's divinity. No one had the right to claim Ibrahim's community — except those who shun shirk.

Ibn Kathir adds a point of balance: commanding the Prophet ﷺ to follow the religion of Ibrahim does not mean Ibrahim reached greater perfection in it. Rather, our Prophet ﷺ established the religion perfectly and it was *completed* for him — which is why he is the Final Prophet, the chief of all the Children of Adam, holder of the station of praise and glory and the honour of intercession, whom all creation — even Ibrahim, the friend of Allah — will seek on the Day of Resurrection to request that Judgement begin. Ibn Kathir also cites the hadith recorded by Imam Ahmad from Ibn ʿAbbas: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked which religion is best with Allah, and he answered, *al-Ḥanīfiyyah as-Samḥah* — the easy monotheism.

## "My prayer, my sacrifice, my living and my dying" (162–163)

**The word nusuk.** Translated "sacrifice" or "worship," *nusuk* has layers. Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān explains that it means the sacrificial offering; it also names everything done in Hajj — hence the rites of Hajj are called *manāsik*, its plural; and it is also used for worship (ʿibādah) in the absolute sense, so that a *nāsik* is simply a devoted worshipper. Mujahid, among the early commentators, took it as the sacrifice offered during Hajj and ʿUmrah. Tafsirs to all these effects are reported from the Companions and their students, but Maʿārif judges the broadest one — all acts of worship — most fitting here: "My prayer, my offerings in worship, my life and my death are all for Allah, the Lord of all the worlds."

**Why this order?** Maʿārif traces the expanding circles. Salah (the ritual prayer) is named first because it is the moving spirit of all good deeds and the pillar of the religion. Then all deeds and acts of worship. Then, wider still, everything done or faced in a lifetime. And the last to be mentioned was death itself. All of it, the verse declares, is for Allah alone, the Lord of all the worlds, who has no associate or partner.

**A pointed defiance.** Ibn Kathir explains that the idolaters used to worship the idols and sacrifice to them, so Allah commanded His Prophet ﷺ to inform those who worship other than Allah and sacrifice to something other than Him that he opposes them in all of it — his prayer is for Allah and his rituals are in His Name alone, just as Allah said elsewhere, "Therefore turn in prayer to your Lord and sacrifice" (108:2). The command is to dedicate intention and heart in pure sincerity to Him.

**What "my life and my death" means.** The declaration that worship is for Allah plainly means it must be free of shirk, hypocrisy, and any worldly interest. As for life and death, Maʿārif offers two readings. One: since my very life and death are in His control, everything I do in them must be for Him alone. Two: the deeds tied to life — prayer, fasting, the rights and duties involved in dealings with people — are for Allah, and the deeds that relate to death — one's will (wasiyyah), the ideal one longs to leave behind — are equally for Allah and subordinate to His command.

**Living the verse.** Maʿārif calls this the outcome of perfect faith and perfect sincerity: to keep present, in every state and every act, the thought — *my Rabb, and the Rabb of the whole world, is one Rabb; I am His servant; I am in His sight at every moment; let not my heart, mind, eyes, ears, tongue, hands, feet, pen or step move against His pleasure.* This is *murāqabah* — watchful awareness of Allah — of the highest order, and whoever trains the heart to hold it finds that sin and disobedience become scared to come anywhere near. In Tafsir ad-Durr al-Manthūr it is reported that the Companion Abu Musa al-Ashʿari said he honestly wished every Muslim would keep reciting this verse time and again, almost as the constant formula of his or her life.

**The Prophet ﷺ prayed with these words.** Imam Ahmad recorded from ʿAli that when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to start the prayer with the takbīr, he would then supplicate: "I have directed my face towards He Who has created the heavens and earth, ḥanīfan, and I am not among the Mushrikin. Certainly, my prayer, sacrifice, living and dying are all for Allah, Lord of the worlds…" — continuing with a plea for forgiveness of all sins and for guidance to the best of conduct, "for none except You directs to the best conduct." This hadith was also recorded by Muslim in the Sahih. The ayah was not an abstract slogan to him ﷺ; it was on his lips at the opening of his prayer.

**"The first of the Muslims" (163).** Qatadah explained: the first *of this Ummah* — and Ibn Kathir calls this a sound meaning, because every prophet before him was also calling to Islam, the worship of Allah alone without partners. Nuh, Ibrahim, Yaʿqub, Yusuf, Musa, and the disciples of ʿIsa all declared themselves Muslims — those who submit — as verse after verse testifies. The Prophet ﷺ expressed this with a memorable image: the prophets are like half-brothers — one father, different mothers. The religion, the one father, is one: worshipping Allah alone without partners; the revealed laws, like the different mothers, differed, and the Law given to Muhammad ﷺ abrogated all before it and will stand with its flags raised high until the Day of Resurrection. Maʿārif adds the reason the prophet of each nation is its "first Muslim": he is the one to whom the revealed code of guidance comes, and so the first to submit to it.

## "Shall I seek a lord other than Allah?" (164)

**The occasion.** Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān records that the disbelievers of Makkah — with Walid ibn Mughirah among them — used to tell the Prophet ﷺ and the Muslims: return to our religion, and *we will carry the burden of all your sins*. Ayah 164 is the answer, and it dismantles the offer twice over.

First: "Shall I seek a lord other than Allah, while He is the Lord of all things?" Ibn Kathir observes that this ayah commands sincerely trusting Allah, while the ayah before it commands sincerely worshipping Him alone without partners — two meanings the Qur'an often mentions together, as in "You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help" (1:5). Why would anyone seek another lord when He is the Lord of everything, Owner of all things, the One who protects and governs all one's affairs?

Second: the offer to carry another's sins is absurd. A sin is written in the record of the one who commits it; it cannot be transferred by someone's mere say-so. "No soul earns except against itself, and no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another." Ibn Kathir explains that this emphasizes Allah's reckoning, decision and perfect justice on the Day of Resurrection: souls recompensed only for their own deeds, good for good and evil for evil, no person carrying another's burden. Scholars of Tafsir, he relates, commented: "No person will be wronged by carrying the evil deeds of another person, nor will his own good deeds be curtailed or decreased." He notes one flow in the *opposite* direction only: by Allah's favour and bounty, the believing offspring who follow their parents in faith are elevated to their parents' grades in Paradise through the blessing of their parents' good works (52:21) — blessing can be shared; sin cannot.

**How the Companions used this ayah.** Maʿārif relates that it was on the authority of this verse that the Prophet ﷺ said that a child born out of wedlock is not affected by the sin of the parents (a hadith reported by Hakim from ʿA'ishah, on sound authority). And when Ibn ʿUmar reported the saying that the crying of the living causes punishment to the deceased, ʿA'ishah answered — with full respect for his integrity, "a person who never lies" — that there are occasions when one does not hear right, and that the decisive verdict of the Qur'an is sufficient: *no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another* — how could another's weeping bring punishment down on the dead for no reason? For them, the verse settled the matter.

The ayah ends: "Then to your Lord is your return, and He will inform you concerning that over which you used to differ." Maʿārif draws the practical point — better to keep verbal confrontation in check and devote more to preparing for the end of things, where every dispute receives its final verdict.

## Successors on the earth, and the sūrah's last word (165)

**Khalāʼif — those who succeed others.** The word is the plural of *khalīfah*, a vice-regent or deputy. Maʿārif unfolds the sobering thought: there is no home, no land you call your private property today that was not, only yesterday, owned by human beings like you. Allah removed them and seated you in their place — generation after generation, century after century, as Ibn Zayd and others explained.

**Ranks raised, as a test.** He has made people differ — in provision, conduct, qualities, appearance and more — and, Ibn Kathir says, His perfect wisdom runs through all of it: Allah tries the rich man concerning his wealth and will ask him how he appreciated it, and tries the poor man concerning his poverty and will ask him about his patience with it. Maʿārif adds: had rank been in anyone's own control, who would have chosen to remain poor and low? The very unevenness of the world points to the One in whose hand honour and provision lie — and turns every blessing into an open question: gratitude and obedience, or ingratitude and disobedience? Muslim recorded that Abu Saʿid al-Khudri said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Verily, this life is beautiful and green, and Allah made you dwell in it generation after generation so that He sees what you will do. Therefore, beware of this life…"

**Swift in retribution — and Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful.** The closing sentence holds warning and hope together, and Ibn Kathir dwells on the pairing: Allah often mentions these two attributes together in the Qur'an — sometimes He calls His servants with encouragement, describing Paradise and making them eager for what He has with Him; sometimes with warning, mentioning the Fire and the Day of Resurrection and its horrors; and sometimes both at once, so that each person is affected according to his or her qualities. He cites the hadith recorded by Imam Ahmad from Abu Hurayrah — also recorded by Muslim and at-Tirmidhi, who graded it "Hasan" — that if the believer knew Allah's punishment, no one would hope in entering His Paradise, and if the disbeliever knew Allah's mercy, no one would feel hopeless of acquiring Paradise; Allah created a hundred kinds of mercy, sent one down among His creation by which they are merciful to one another, and with Him remain ninety-nine. And in another narration from Abu Hurayrah, the Prophet ﷺ said that when Allah created the creation He wrote in a Book that is with Him above the Throne: "My mercy overcomes My anger."

**The seal of al-Anʿām.** Maʿārif observes that the sūrah opened with *ḥamd* — the praise of Allah — and closes on *maghfirah* — the seeking of His forgiveness. It also relates the hadith that Sūrah al-Anʿām was revealed all at one time, with seventy thousand angels following it, glorifying Allah — which is why ʿUmar al-Faruq counted it among the highly merited sūrahs of the Qur'an. Fitting, then, that its final passage is the believer's whole creed in miniature: guided by my Lord, on the religion of Ibrahim; my prayer, my worship, my life and my death for Allah alone; no lord sought besides Him; answerable only for my own deeds; placed on this earth as a successor under trial — before a Lord swift in reckoning, and Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful.
